title: Public adminModuleCall exposes jackpot payout delegatecall
description: The commit adds LotteryManager4626.adminModuleCall(bytes) as an unrestricted external wrapper around _adminModule.delegatecall(data). The admin module contains payoutLocalJackpot(address,address,uint16), which is intentionally external and onlyDelegateCall because it was previously reachable only from the manager's internal _payoutLocalJackpot path. It does not have onlyOwner or any validation that a real lottery win occurred. Because adminModuleCall performs the delegatecall from the LotteryManager address, onlyDelegateCall passes, and subsequent gaugeController.payJackpot calls see msg.sender as the legitimate LotteryManager. Any unauthenticated caller can therefore call adminModuleCall(abi.encodeWithSelector(LotteryManager4626AdminModule.payoutLocalJackpot.selector, token, attacker, 10000)) to pay 100% of an active token's jackpot reserve to an arbitrary winner address. With singleVaultJackpotOnly enabled this drains the specified triggering coin's reserve; if multi-vault mode is enabled it can drain reserves across the scan window.

title: Default auto-keep can SSRF and pin internal responses
description: New Hermit auto-keep processing is enabled by default and is scheduled for every newly ingested live or history message in Hermit command rooms. If a message has a keepable attachment from a hex sender, the new code passes the attachment URL to keepHermitMemeFromMedia, which ultimately calls pinRemoteMediaToPinata. That fetcher only requires the original URL to start with https:// and uses redirect: 'follow' without DNS/IP/private-range validation or a final-URL scheme/host check. It also accepts media based on the original filename/extension even if the fetched response content type is not an image. As a result, a room participant can post an attachment such as an attacker-controlled https:// URL with a .gif path that redirects to an internal HTTP/HTTPS endpoint; if the response is under 12 MB, the backend will upload the bytes to Pinata and store a public 4626.fun/ipfs URL. This can turn the server into an SSRF oracle with potential exfiltration of internal services or metadata endpoints. The low-level fetcher behavior existed before for manual /keep, but this commit introduces a default-on unattended trigger for ordinary media drops.

title: SSRF in Hermit /keep media pinning
description: The commit introduces a new `/keep` command that is open to AlfaClub room users and passes reply attachment URLs into `keepHermitMemeFromMedia()`. `isKeepableMediaAttachment()` accepts any HTTPS URL when the attachment claims an image type/mime or has an image-looking filename. `pinRemoteMediaToPinata()` then fetches that URL with `redirect: 'follow'`, performs no hostname allowlist, private IP/DNS checks, or per-redirect validation, and accepts arbitrary response bytes if the original URL or supplied filename looks like an image. The fetched bytes are uploaded to Pinata and the resulting public IPFS URL is returned to the chat. An attacker who can cause a replied attachment to reference `https://attacker.example/x.gif` redirecting to an internal HTTP/HTTPS service, or directly reference an internal HTTPS endpoint with `filename=secret.gif`, can make the backend fetch internal resources and publish the response bytes to IPFS. This bypasses the repository's existing SSRF patterns used by the external image proxy, which manually validates DNS/IPs and redirects before fetching.

title: Chip username spoof bypasses staker trade gate
description: The new Chip handling treats `message.username` equal to `chip` or `chipbot` as sufficient to parse a structured trade card, even when the actual `sender` is a normal user wallet. Once parsed, `resolveInverseAkitaTradeEventAuthor` prefers `payloadAddress` without verifying that the message came from the real `trade-completed` system sender or that the payload address belongs to the chat sender. The resulting attributed wallet is then passed to `resolveInverseAkitaChatAuthorAccess`, which performs the staker eligibility check, and if eligible the code submits a real Arena/Hyperliquid trade. Therefore an attacker who can post to the room can set their display username to `Chip`/`chipbot` and send JSON such as `{"coin":"BTC","dir":"Open Long","userAddress":"0x<eligible-staker>"}`. The bot will attribute the intent to the victim staker and execute the inverse trade from the shared executor wallet. This is an authorization bypass of the staker gate and can cause unauthorized trading/losses, bounded by configured trade size/cooldowns but repeatable across eligible addresses.

title: trade-completed payload can spoof chat reaction author
description: Before this change, inverse chat reactions only accepted messages whose sender was a valid wallet address. The new path explicitly exempts `sender=trade-completed` from that sender validation, parses the chat text as JSON, and assigns `sender` from `tradeEvent.userAddress` or from `readRoomLabelStatus()`'s room creator fallback. `executeInverseAkitaChatReaction()` then uses that attributed sender for `resolveInverseAkitaChatAuthorAccess()`, which is the stake gate before executing Arena trades. The code does not cryptographically or structurally verify that the payload `userAddress` is the actual trade author, that the system post is authentic, or that a no-wallet payload should be authorized as the room creator. It also skips self-sender filtering for the post-attribution wallet. If an attacker can inject/poison a room history or websocket message with `sender: "trade-completed"` and a market-open JSON payload, they can spoof an eligible staker or room creator and trigger the bot's trading wallet to open/trim/add positions.

title: Auto-discovered rooms can trigger strategy trades
description: The new dynamic room discovery path reads wallets from env/JWT, queries their AlfaClub FriendKey holdings, maps every held tokenId directly to a reaction room id, and installs those rooms into the runtime reaction-room set. The bridge then polls all reaction rooms and processes inverse chat intents from them. Since author access only requires the sender to have stake in a configured reaction room, an attacker-controlled room that becomes auto-discovered can satisfy the room check and lead to `runArenaTrade` using the strategy execution config. AlfaClub keys are transferable ERC-1155-style holdings, so relying on wallet holdings alone is not an authorization boundary: unsolicited or attacker-provided keys can expand the bot's trusted execution surface. The removed fixed-room allowlist also means there is no safety net limiting execution to known rooms.

title: Self-bundled deploys overfund user-withdrawable deposits
description: The new self-bundling path calculates a required prefund from the forced high gas limits, adds a 10% buffer, and sends the shortfall to EntryPoint.depositTo(sender). EntryPoint deposits belong to the sender account, not to the funder or to a specific UserOp. Any gas not actually consumed, the explicit 10% buffer, and in some failure cases the entire prefund remain credited to the user's Coinbase Smart Wallet. Since the user controls that smart wallet, they can later execute EntryPoint.withdrawTo and extract the leftover ETH. This is made worse because withDeploySessionUserOpGas forces all deploy-session operations above the self-bundle threshold, while the changed call sites omit CDP paymaster sponsorship for those operations. The service therefore uses DEPLOY_SESSION_SELF_BUNDLE_PRIVATE_KEY, or even fallback operational keys PRIVATE_KEY/KPR_PRIVATE_KEY, as an open top-up source for user-controlled EntryPoint balances.

title: Cross-room stake grants shared executor trade authority
description: The new policy no longer requires the author to be the on-chain room owner for extra reaction rooms or to have stake in the room where the message was posted. Instead, resolveInverseAkitaChatAuthorAccess builds a list containing the message room plus all configured reaction rooms, and returns eligible as soon as readUserStakedKeys reports at least one key in any candidate room. Because executeInverseAkitaChatReaction then uses that eligibility to route the resulting order through the shared room-1659 executor identity, an attacker who can acquire or temporarily stake one FriendKey in any watched room can post market-opinion text in any watched reaction room and cause the shared bot wallet to submit leveraged trades. The authorization is therefore cross-room and not scoped to the room that produced the trigger. This is an access-control regression relative to the previous owner-only gating for rooms 1484/1660/2/1043 and room-1659-only stake gate.

title: Paymaster accepts phase-2 code IDs for wrong vault lane
description: The commit changes phase-2 paymaster validation to accept either the Creator or Agent code-id tuple. However, the validator does not prove that the tuple matches the lane of the existing phase-1 deployment. It derives a lane from the submitted vault codeId for CREATE2 validation, but if that check fails it falls back to matching a Phase1Deployed event only by token/owner/vault/wrapper/shareOFT, not by vaultKind or codeIds. As a result, a Creator phase-1 vault can be submitted with Agent phase-2 codeIds, or vice versa, and still pass the proxy's sponsorship filter. The on-chain batcher then deploys the submitted gauge bytecode but wires it using the persisted phase-1 vaultKind; a cross-lane tuple will revert when the batcher calls the wrong lane-specific setter. This creates a paymaster policy bypass and sponsorship-drain vector: authenticated attackers can craft UserOps that pass offchain validation but consume sponsored gas during reverted phase-2 execution.

title: Bootstrap helper can overwrite Solana peer bindings
description: RegistryBootstrap4626 is intended to be deployed as an authorized Registry4626 factory whose owner can only perform first-time token wiring. That first-set-only invariant is true for vault/wrapper/shareOFT/oracle/gauge fields because Registry4626 routes them through _requireBindingWritable. However, the new helper also exposes setOmnichainMesh and setSolanaShareOFTPeer paths, and its reconcile functions call Registry4626.setOmnichainVaultMesh and setRemoteOFTPeerBytes32 whenever the current value differs. Those registry setters are only gated by onlyAuthorizedOrOwner and do not enforce the live-rebind/owner-only protection. As a result, once this helper is authorized, the helper owner can overwrite an already configured Solana asset/share mesh or Solana ShareOFT peer for any registered token. DeploymentBatcher later trusts the registry peer and can propagate it into the actual ShareOFT LayerZero peer, so a compromised or lower-trust bootstrap-owner key can redirect cross-chain share routing/configuration without registry-owner live rebind.

title: Ajna keepers can move vault buffer into risky buckets
description: AjnaERC4626Vault.moveFromBuffer previously required onlyAdapterAuthorized, meaning only the configured swapper/adapter could move idle buffer assets into Ajna buckets. This commit changes it to onlySwapperOrKeeper. Because keepers are independently configurable automation addresses, a compromised or malicious keeper can now call moveFromBuffer directly and choose any bucket index that passes only the broad range/minBucket checks. This can move most idle liquidity out of the buffer into attacker-chosen Ajna exposure, reducing withdraw liquidity and potentially placing vault assets into unfavorable or toxic buckets without going through the strategy adapter or management policy. The buffer-ratio guard limits complete drainage but does not prevent economically harmful bucket selection.

title: Privy signing key synced to non-production Vercel envs
description: The commit adds PRIVY_WALLET_AUTHORIZATION_KEY and related Privy publisher variables to the Vercel env sync script, but applies them inside the existing loop over production, preview, and development targets. PRIVY_WALLET_AUTHORIZATION_KEY is treated by the backend as a private key used to sign Privy wallet API requests. If preview or development deployments can run unreviewed branch code, be accessed by broader operators, or otherwise have weaker controls than production, those deployments can read the same privileged authorization key and use it outside the intended production trust boundary. This can lead to compromise of the Privy server-wallet signing authority used by privileged publisher/agent workflows. The shim file itself appears to be a benign re-export.

title: First LP seed can use a manipulated V4 pool price
description: Previously, CCA migration atomically initialized the V4 pool and minted the initial LP position at the auction clearing price. This commit changes migrate() so it only initializes the pool and marks the launch migrated, while retaining the ShareOFT reserve and raised currency for a later seedLpManager()/seedRebalance() flow. The new OVaultLPManager.seedRebalance() path does not call checkCanRebalance(), so it skips the TWAP oracle, current-vs-TWAP deviation, minimum movement, and boundary checks. It then reads the current pool tick and deploys the retained balances into full/base/limit ranges around that tick. Because the pool may have no protocol liquidity after migrate(), an unprivileged attacker can add small liquidity and trade the pool to an artificial tick before the keeper calls seedRebalance(). The keeper then seeds the protocol's launch liquidity at this manipulated price. The slippage check only compares the raw ASSET balance after minting and does not protect the paired ETH/currency side, so manipulating the seed to consume/expose the paired side can still pass and allow extraction/arbitrage of launch liquidity.

title: `/h arena` bypasses Hermit operator authorization
description: The command dispatcher enforces the Hermit operator allowlist by calling `isHermitOperatorOnlyCommand(raw)` before `executeHermitCommand` remaps aliases. This commit adds `h` as a Hermit alias and maps `/h arena ...` to the internal `/arena` command, but `isHermitOperatorOnlyCommand` still checks only raw `/arena`, `/signal`, and `/strategy bias`. As a result, `/h arena long ...`, `/h arena bridge ...`, `/h arena transfer ...`, etc. are not classified as operator-only. Once inside `executeHermitCommand`, the Arena branch only checks that the chat room is in the Arena allowed-room list, then runs privileged Arena operations using the configured bot/agent credentials. In live deployments with Arena enabled and trading/funding enabled, a regular room participant could submit trades or move funds without being an OWNER/ADMIN, allowlisted Hermit user, or `HERMIT_OWNER_ADDRESS`.

title: External EOA fallback can bypass swap paymaster policy
description: The new Swap.tsx fallback treats any connected EOA that is an on-chain owner of a non-platform CSW as a canonical signer whenever the embedded Privy signer gate is not ready. That makes the swap router pass this external wallet client and signer address into the canonical execution path. For such non-Privy signers, txRouter selects canonical4337 with canonicalDirect as a fallback, and it also explicitly falls back to canonicalDirect for native-value router calls or certain paymaster policy failures. canonicalDirect then ABI-encodes the API-provided approval/swap calls directly into Coinbase Smart Wallet executeBatch and asks the EOA to send the transaction to the CSW. The transaction payload is only checked for syntactic validity, not against the paymaster allowlist of permitted swap targets/selectors or against expected swap semantics. If an upstream swap API response, proxy, or frontend response is malicious, it can cause a user-owned CSW owner to sign an opaque executeBatch that transfers or approves arbitrary CSW assets, bypassing the server-side paymaster validation that normally constrains sponsored canonical swaps.

title: Wallet-first waitlist login can trust spoofed email hints
description: The new waitlist login option selection treats either a stored verified-email hint or a positive `cv:privy:lastAuthAt` localStorage value as enough to offer wallet-first Privy login. Both values are client-controlled/stale hints, not proof that the next Privy token contains a verified email. After a wallet-only login, the waitlist bootstrap pipeline still includes `verifiedEmailHint` in the `/api/waitlist/bootstrap` body. The backend then falls back from `extractPrivyVerifiedEmail(privyUser)` to this body email hint, and later uses that derived `resolvedEmail` to upsert an account with `emailVerified: true` and to rebind email-collision profiles through the waitlist hint adoption path. This means the commit introduces an official UI path where an attacker can combine their own wallet-authenticated Privy token with a spoofed/stale waitlist email hint. The server-side hint-trust weakness existed already as a public API issue, but the commit newly pairs it with wallet-only sign-in in the waitlist flow instead of forcing email OTP first.

title: Privy proxy leaks parent-domain session cookie
description: This commit adds a host-based route that rewrites every request for privy.4626.fun to https://auth.privy.io/$1. The application session cookie is named cv_auth_session and, on production 4626 hosts, is intentionally set with Domain=.4626.fun. Therefore any browser request to privy.4626.fun, including normal custom-auth-domain SDK traffic, iframe/navigation traffic, or a user clicking a link, will include the 4626 application session cookie. Because the Vercel external rewrite acts as a proxy to auth.privy.io, that Cookie header is forwarded outside the 4626 trust boundary. HttpOnly does not help because the browser still transmits the cookie on matching-domain requests, and SameSite=Strict does not help because privy.4626.fun and app.4626.fun are same-site. A recipient or compromise of the upstream service/logging path could replay the leaked session token against 4626 APIs; outside the browser, the Origin header guard can be spoofed. The route should not proxy requests carrying parent-domain app cookies to a third party. Use a host-only __Host- session cookie, move the auth custom domain to a separate site, or implement a controlled proxy that strips application cookies and prevents upstream Set-Cookie Domain=.4626.fun cookie tossing.

title: User HL API key leaks to arena child processes
description: The commit introduces ALFACLUB_COUNTER_TRADE_USER_HL_AGENT_KEY as a long-lived Hyperliquid API-wallet private key. arenaClient executes dgclaw/acp child processes with an environment built from the full parent process.env plus command-specific overrides. For the bot/ACP lane, buildArenaCommandEnv only blanks HL_AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY, but it does not remove the original ALFACLUB_COUNTER_TRADE_USER_HL_AGENT_KEY variable. As a result, any arena child process, including ACP commands, npx/tsx, patched dgclaw scripts, or compromised dependencies loaded by those commands, can read the user's API-wallet private key from its environment. The key is described as trade-only, but disclosure still enables arbitrary order placement on the approved Hyperliquid account and can cause large financial loss.

title: Untrusted quote output sets external swap min-out
description: When PAYOUT_ROUTER_ALLOW_EXTERNAL_SWAPS is enabled, the commit adds best-effort parsing of amountOut from the external quote response and uses that value, minus slippage, as minCreatorOut for convertViaExternalAndQueue. This is not an independent slippage check: the attacker-controlled external quote response also provides swapTarget, spender, and swapCallData. If the response supplies an approved target/spender, malicious calldata that spends the router's full tokenIn balance, and a tiny amountOut such as 1, the keeper will submit minCreatorOut=1. The PayoutRouter only checks that creatorOut >= minCreatorOut, so the transaction can succeed while converting a valuable ZORA/WETH balance into a negligible amount of creator coin. Before this change, the default minCreatorOut of 0 would revert in the contract for external swaps unless operators configured an explicit floor.

title: Hermit Telegram token can mint Mini App sessions
description: Telegram Mini App initData is authenticated only by an HMAC derived from the bot token. This commit adds ALFACLUB_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN to the accepted token candidates for /api/telegram/miniapp-session and even reports Mini App auth as configured when only that token is present. ALFACLUB_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN is used elsewhere as the Hermit/AlfaClub relay bot token, not as the canonical Telegram account-linking bot token. Anyone who has or compromises this narrower-scope relay bot token can compute valid initData hashes offline for arbitrary Telegram user IDs/usernames, obtain a Mini App session token, and use that session in downstream Telegram identity flows such as account linking or Zora CSW gate verification. This increases the blast radius of the Hermit relay secret and breaks token scope separation.

title: Hermit DMs expose privileged command executor
description: The commit adds a private-chat path for the Hermit Telegram webhook. Its default configuration enables DMs and treats an empty allowlist as allowing every Telegram user. For DM text, it passes any slash command through unchanged, then calls executeDeterministicCommand with an AlfaClub room chatId and a sender wallet resolved directly from the Telegram env mapping/default wallet. This bypasses the existing Telegram private-DM safeguards that force non-admin private DMs to the zero address and block sensitive commands such as /send, /coin create, /coin deploy, /lock, and /unlock. It also bypasses the AlfaClub bridge's narrower command filter, which only routes help/alfaclub/hermit command families from room messages. As a result, anyone who can DM the Hermit bot can attempt arbitrary deterministic command families such as /send, /coin, /x post --confirm, or /alfa buy-key/create-room/brief-post in the configured AlfaClub room context. In deployments where TELEGRAM_DEFAULT_SENDER_WALLET or a Telegram user map resolves to an admin/execution-ready wallet, this can lead to unauthorized onchain transfers/trades/AlfaClub key purchases or unauthorized social posting. Even when privileged execution fails, the public DM path exposes internal room-scoped command behavior that was previously gated.

title: Unverified Solana mint mapping can hijack keeper routing
description: The new deployment flow reads `payload.solanaOvault.shareMeshMint`, stores it with the ShareOFT decoded from the phase-2 finalize calldata, and queues a keeper/orchestrator sync. The deployment create path only preserves `shareMeshMint` as a non-empty string, and the new sync path only validates Solana-address syntax; neither path checks the on-chain bridge adapter's registered `tokenToSolanaMint(shareOft)`, the Solana program creator config, or any existing mint ownership. The DB also has uniqueness only on `share_oft`, not on `share_mesh_mint`, and the orchestrator merge uses `{ ...currentMapping, [shareMeshMint]: shareOft }`, silently overwriting an existing mapping for the same mint. Because keeper workflows later trust `SOLANA_SHARE_OFT_MAPPING[mint]` when building lottery entries and fee forwarding calls, an authenticated deployer who completes an OVault deployment can point a victim Solana mint at the attacker's ShareOFT. This can corrupt cross-chain lottery attribution, break or redirect keeper accounting, and cause availability/integrity failures for the legitimate mint.

title: Workflow dispatch input allows secret-bearing shell injection
description: The workflow defines `slot` and `dry_run` as free-form `workflow_dispatch` strings and then embeds them directly into `run:` bash blocks using GitHub expression substitution. GitHub substitutes `${{ inputs.* }}` and `${{ steps.resolve.outputs.* }}` before bash parses the script, so an input containing quotes and shell metacharacters can break out of the intended string. The first `Resolve slot` step writes the attacker-controlled value to `GITHUB_OUTPUT`; the later `Run ACP daily market-news runner` step interpolates those outputs inside a bash script while ACP access/refresh tokens, owner wallet, and agent id are present in the environment. The runner script's own `--slot` validation cannot prevent this, because command injection occurs before the script is invoked. An attacker with permission to manually dispatch this workflow could exfiltrate ACP credentials or perform unauthorized ACP/onchain job funding actions from CI.

title: Counter-trade opt-in can trade the room default Arena wallet
description: The new counter-trade feature intentionally leaves `/strategy optin` open to non-operator room users, but the opt-in check only rejects `env_default` identities. `resolveArenaIdentityForContext` falls back from a caller-specific mapping to the room-default `'*'` mapping, whose `source` is `room_default`. Because `room_default` passes the `identity.source !== 'env_default'` check, an ordinary room member can opt in without owning or registering a personal Arena identity. The cron runner then resolves the identity again for that sender and uses the returned `agentId`/`agentWalletAddress` to call `runArenaTrade`. If a trusted operator configured a room-default Arena agent, the attacker's opt-in can therefore cause trades on that shared/default agent. If the room default also has an `hlApiWalletAddress`, the same upstream fills can be processed once per opted-in sender because the event ledger key is scoped by `senderAddress`, multiplying trades against the same default wallet. The opt-in path should require a caller-specific `identity.source === 'user'` mapping, or otherwise bind and verify the exact user-owned Arena identity at opt-in and at execution time; room-default identities should not be usable by arbitrary opt-ins.

title: dgclaw submodule retargeted to untrusted fork
description: This commit retargets the dgclaw-skill submodule URL from the upstream Virtual-Protocol repository to https://github.com/wenakita/dgclaw-skill.git and advances the gitlink to f3e23d1a208a14a7993753e88441344281956603. dgclaw-skill is not a passive dependency: the Arena integration resolves dgclaw.sh and scripts under ARENA_DGCLAW_DIR, executes them with execFile, and passes the server process environment through to the child process. Those live commands include join, activate-unified-account, add-api-wallet, deposit, and trade flows, and the environment is expected to contain DGCLAW_API_KEY and may contain ACP access/refresh tokens or trading credentials. Moving this executable dependency to a personal fork bypasses upstream review and gives the forked dependency control over code that can run inside the privileged backend runtime, potentially exfiltrating secrets or submitting unauthorized ACP/Arena/Hyperliquid actions when Arena commands are executed. I could not initialize the submodule in this environment because outbound GitHub access is blocked, so the specific contents of the new submodule commit could not be reviewed; the security issue introduced by the superproject commit is the trust-boundary change for executable runtime code.

title: Unpinned external CLI and skill code in production image
description: The commit adds a production-image build step that installs the latest @virtuals-protocol/acp-cli from npm and clones dgclaw-skill from an external GitHub repository using the mutable default ref `main`. It then runs `npm install --omit=dev` inside that cloned repository with npm lifecycle scripts enabled. None of these artifacts are pinned by version, commit hash, lockfile, digest, checksum, or signature. This means a later rebuild can silently include different code than was reviewed in this repository. If the npm package, the GitHub repository, or any dependency install script is compromised, arbitrary code can execute during the image build and the compromised CLI/skill code is also baked into the production runtime. The impact is amplified because the existing Arena client executes `dgclaw.sh`, node scripts, and `acp` commands from the configured dgclaw directory while inheriting process environment variables, which may include ACP refresh/access tokens and trading/agent credentials. This is not directly exploitable by an ordinary HTTP user without a supply-chain compromise or malicious build configuration, but it creates a high-impact supply-chain RCE and secret-exfiltration path for the Hermit/Arena runtime.

title: CRE shadow-mode can be bypassed by authenticated callers
description: The commit introduces CRE attestation endpoints with environment flags intended to keep Solana NAV and oracle lanes in shadow/monitor-only mode. However, the handlers allow the caller-controlled body field `forceWrite` to override `CRE_SOLANA_NAV_SHADOW_ONLY` and `CRE_ORACLE_SHADOW_ONLY`. In addition, the direct Solana NAV update endpoint only checks `CRE_SOLANA_NAV_WRITE_ENABLED` and `CRE_KILL_SWITCH`; it does not check `CRE_SOLANA_NAV_SHADOW_ONLY` at all before using `KPR_PRIVATE_KEY` to submit `updateRemoteNav`. As a result, an authenticated external attestation submitter or compromised `KPR_API_KEY` can cause keeper-signed on-chain writes while operators believe shadow mode is preventing writes. This undermines the rollout guardrails and can affect vault/oracle accounting within the on-chain caps.

title: Swap sponsorship bypasses creator allowlist
description: The commit changed `validateSponsoredSmartWalletCalls` so `validated.mode === 'swap'` skips `assertCreatorAllowlisted`. The allowlist function still enforces Supabase/Postgres/env allowlists for other modes, but swap mode now returns directly after shape validation. Because the swap classifier only requires a single allowed router call that references a known token, and the allowed Universal Router commands include Permit2 and wrap/unwrap commands as well as swaps, a non-allowlisted user with a valid session for their Coinbase Smart Wallet can submit sponsored Universal Router operations and have the upstream paymaster/bundler pay gas. This bypasses the paymaster's access-control policy and can be abused to drain sponsorship budget or degrade availability for legitimate users despite the per-session rate limit.

title: CSW Permit2 signing trusts unvalidated quote permit data
description: Before this commit, canonical CSW swaps disabled Permit2. The new path explicitly keeps Permit2 enabled when the execution address is the canonical CSW, then `signPermit2ForExecutionWallet` parses externally supplied `permitData` and, for a deployed smart-wallet owner, creates an ERC-1271-compatible CSW signature over that digest. The code only checks that `details.token` and `spender` are syntactically valid addresses so it can read a nonce; it does not enforce that the EIP-712 domain is Base Permit2, that the primary type is the expected PermitSingle shape, that the spender is a known Uniswap router, or that the permit amount/token/deadline match the quote the user requested. Under the repository threat model, quote/API responses are attacker-controlled inputs. A malicious quote response could request a Permit2 allowance for an attacker-controlled spender or excessive amount, obtain a CSW-valid signature, and then use Permit2 to drain that token from the smart wallet.

title: Historical embedded EOA re-enabled for CSW execution
description: The previous policy separated broad identity/owner recognition from the stricter execution signer set for the canonical CSW. This commit adds `0xceca13f2686ed061c57620ecdf67e1b8c0f285e9`—documented here as a Privy embedded EOA—directly to `CANONICAL_CSW_EXECUTION_OWNER_ADDRESSES`. Both the transaction router and the ERC-4337 sender rely on `isAllowedCanonicalCswExecutionSigner`, so this address now passes the hard execution gate for `CANONICAL_CSW_ADDRESS`. If this historical embedded EOA or its Privy session is compromised, stale, shared, or otherwise less controlled than the active automation/admin owners, an attacker can use first-party canonical4337 execution paths to submit swaps, approvals, or other allowed CSW calls from the canonical wallet. Because the canonical CSW is also used as profile identity, XMTP identity, and vault owner, this materially increases the blast radius of that historical key.

title: Missing RLS on condensed sensitive Supabase tables
description: Several runtime schema bootstraps that previously created sensitive tables and immediately enabled deny-all Row Level Security now only delegate to new migration files. The new migrations create tables such as agent_message_memory, episodic_summaries, wallet_intelligence_cache, feedback_index, and Zora CSW gate token/challenge tables without any ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY or deny-all CREATE POLICY statements. On Supabase, public-schema tables without RLS can be exposed through the REST API to clients holding the public anon key. This can leak private agent conversation memory, wallet intelligence graphs, labels, and gate-token metadata, and may allow tampering with persistent agent memory or operational gate state. Older RLS migrations are timestamped before these newly added CREATE TABLE migrations and use ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS, so they do not protect tables that are first created by these new migrations or by the new runtime delegation path.

title: Unauthenticated Relay quote proxy exposes subsidized arbitrary intents
description: The new relay/quote route is reachable from the public catch-all API and only applies an IP rate limit. It does not require a session, Privy token, SIWE/SIWA principal, deploy session, or ownership proof. The handler explicitly accepts any 20-byte `to`, arbitrary hex calldata, caller-controlled `user`/`recipient`, and caller-controlled origin/destination chain IDs, then forwards that payload to Relay with `subsidizeFees: true` and the server-side Relay API key when configured. The paired public relay/notify-deposit route similarly lets unauthenticated callers wake Relay indexing/solver APIs using the same backend credential. An attacker can therefore use this app as an open Relay credential/subsidy proxy for arbitrary call-execution quotes, rather than only for the intended add-owner CSW self-call. This can drain or abuse the protocol's Relay quota/subsidy budget, attribute arbitrary traffic to the project, and potentially cause Relay solver activity for attacker-chosen transactions once the attacker submits the required deposit.

title: Unverified waitlist email hints can rebind accounts
description: The new waitlist hint code reads email addresses from Privy user objects without requiring a verified flag, and also falls back to a sessionStorage value. That value is sent as the `email` field to `/api/waitlist/bootstrap`. The bootstrap handler then falls back from `extractPrivyVerifiedEmail(...)` to this client-supplied hint and, if present, calls `upsertAccount(..., emailVerified: true)` and `upsertBootstrapProfile(...)`. For an email already bound to another Privy DID, the collision-adoption helper can also rebind the profile/account when the bootstrap hint matches the collision email, without independently proving that the current Privy user verified that email. An attacker with any valid Privy session can submit or cause the client to submit a victim email as the bootstrap hint, causing the server to treat it as verified and potentially take over an existing waitlist/account identity.

title: Client email hint enables waitlist account takeover
description: Before this change, canonical account email and email-collision rebinds were based on server-observed Privy verified email or ownership checks. The new flow sets `privyEmail` to `bootstrapEmailHint` whenever `extractPrivyVerifiedEmail(privyUser)` is absent, where `bootstrapEmailHint` is just the normalized request body `email`. That value is then passed to `assertNoEmailPrivyCollision`, `upsertAccount` with `emailVerified: true`, and `upsertBootstrapProfile`. Worse, the new `adoptWaitlistBootstrapEmailHintRebind` path treats a matching bootstrap hint as sufficient authorization to rebind an `EMAIL_BOUND_TO_DIFFERENT_PRIVY_USER` collision, calling `rebindEmailCollisionProfile`, which updates both `profiles.privy_user_id` and `accounts.privy_user_id` to the requester. Because the hint is sent by the frontend as JSON body data and is not cryptographically bound to the Privy token, an attacker can call the endpoint directly with their own valid Privy token and an arbitrary victim email.

title: Email rebind leaves stale Privy aliases active
description: The commit adds waitlist-specific collision adoption for users who prove the same verified email in a new Privy session. The actual rebind updates profiles.privy_user_id and accounts.privy_user_id to the new Privy user and inserts a linked email method for the new user. However, the code does not delete the old collision.existingPrivyUserId alias from privy_user_aliases, nor does it upsert an alias for the new Privy user. Other account/profile resolvers explicitly resolve a Privy user by either an alias row or profiles.privy_user_id. In deployments where aliases have been seeded from prior profile rows, the old Privy user id remains mapped to the same profile even after the profile is rebound to the new Privy user. This means a stale/compromised old Privy session can continue accessing alias-aware profile state after the verified-email recovery/rebind succeeds, undermining the recovery flow and allowing unauthorized reads or profile mutations through endpoints that rely on alias-aware profile resolution.

title: Safe helper wire script trusts unvalidated RPC helper slots
description: frontend/scripts/ops/wire-phase3-helper-safe.ts only checks that --phase3-helper is syntactically an address, then reads phase2Module, uniV4Helper, and utilsHelper from the configured RPC endpoint and encodes all four values into a protocol-treasury Safe transaction. It immediately executes that Safe transaction. The on-chain wireDeploymentHelpers sink simply assigns these helper slots and does not validate nonzero addresses, code hashes, helper batcher immutables, or expected canonical addresses. If an operator is pointed at a malicious/compromised RPC endpoint, suffers DNS/RPC MITM, or is given a malicious handoff helper address, the script can cause the Safe owner to sign and execute a transaction that wires attacker-controlled helper contracts. This is particularly dangerous for phase2Module because the batcher later delegatecalls it, allowing malicious code to execute in the DeploymentBatcher storage context during future deployment flows.

title: Paymaster accepts under-validated Zora router calldata
description: The new Zora Universal Router path recognizes selector 0x24856bc3 and treats it as a sponsored swap. Unlike the existing execute(bytes,bytes[],uint256) path, it does not ABI-decode the call, does not require canonical encoding, does not check that command bytes and inputs line up, and does not enforce the existing allowed Universal Router opcode set. When there is no separate approval call, it infers the swap input token by searching the entire raw calldata for a configured USDC or Zora token address. An attacker who can reach the paymaster can include that token address in unused/trailing calldata or in an irrelevant input and submit arbitrary execute(bytes,bytes[]) Universal Router commands, including commands intentionally excluded by the prior opcode allowlist, or malformed calls that pass paymaster validation but revert during execution. This is a paymaster policy bypass and can lead to sponsored execution outside the intended canonical Zora USDC-to-creator swap flow and gas budget exhaustion.

title: Devnet probe spills SOLANA_PRIVATE_KEY to /tmp
description: The commit adds operational guidance and wiring for `ops:pipe-a-devnet-rehearsal`, and changes `kpr/scripts/solana/cost-probe-devnet.ts` so `SOLANA_PRIVATE_KEY` is accepted as the payer key when `COST_PROBE_KEYPAIR` is unset. The script then writes the loaded payer secret key to `/tmp/4626-devnet-cost-probe.json` using `writeFileSync` without an explicit 0600 mode or a private temporary directory. On typical systems this creates a predictable file subject to the process umask, often world-readable as 0644. Because the docs now explicitly tell operators to set `SOLANA_PRIVATE_KEY`, a real privileged Solana key can be copied into `/tmp` during a devnet rehearsal. A local attacker or another process on a shared runner/workstation could read the file and compromise the key.

title: Unpaid Stripe bundle grants deploy entitlements
description: This commit adds the vault_full_deploy bundle and expands it into all deploy entitlements. However, the Stripe checkout endpoint creates a creator_strategy_features row with status='pending' before the creator pays. The Phase 3 deploy-session policy and paymaster weight gate both consume helpers that treat status IN ('pending','active') as entitled and do not require payment_verified_at IS NOT NULL. Because expandCreatorFeatureKeys maps vault_full_deploy to charm_active_lp and ajna_sleeve, an authenticated attacker can start a $499 Stripe checkout for vault_full_deploy, abandon payment, then immediately request/sponsor a Phase 3 deploy with the bundled strategy weights. This bypasses the paid deploy gate and can cause unauthorized/sponsored deployment of premium strategy infrastructure.

title: Batcher can hijack uninitialized registry entries
description: The commit added `_ensureRegistryAndShareOftPeerWired()` to `finalizePhase2Execution()`. `finalizePhase2()` only authenticates `msg.sender == params.owner` and verifies that the supplied vault/wrapper/shareOFT came from this batcher's Phase 1 for `(creatorToken, params.owner, version)`. It does not check the existing `CreatorRegistry.CreatorCoinInfo.creator`. If a creator token is already registered in `CreatorRegistry` but its vault/wrapper/shareOFT/gauge/oracle fields are still zero, any address can deploy a Phase 1 stack for that token under themselves, deposit the required tokens, and finalize. The new code will then set the registry's official vault, wrapper, shareOFT, gauge, and oracle for that pre-registered token to the attacker's deployment. Because the code only writes when fields are zero and does not revert on creator mismatch, the legitimate registered creator can be squatted/hijacked until privileged registry/batcher intervention overwrites or repairs the mapping. Since the registry is used as a trust root for vault/OFT discovery and cross-chain peer wiring, this is an integrity vulnerability in creator-token registration.

title: Safe owner private key can be sent as a Safe tx hash
description: The new frontend/scripts/ops/execute-pending-safe-txs.ts helper accepts a Safe owner private key via --safe-owner-pk. It separately derives safeTxHash inputs by filtering all of process.argv for any string starting with 0x and length 66. A normal 0x-prefixed Ethereum private key is also 66 characters, so running the documented style of command with --safe-owner-pk 0x... causes the private key to be included in hashArgs. The script then calls apiKit.getTransaction(safeTxHash) for every value in hashArgs, transmitting the private key as a transaction hash to the Safe API and any intervening logs/proxies. Exposure of a Safe owner private key can compromise treasury operations, especially for low-threshold Safes or combined with other signer compromise. The script should parse positional safeTxHash arguments explicitly, exclude option values, prefer environment/keystore-based signing, and never treat --safe-owner-pk's value as a transaction hash.

title: Client exposes direct CDP paymaster endpoint
description: The commit adds a client-side owner-install path that reads `import.meta.env.VITE_CDP_SENDCALLS_PAYMASTER_URL`, requires it to be an HTTP(S) direct CDP RPC URL, and passes it into `wallet_prepareCalls` as `capabilities.paymasterService.url`. Vite `VITE_*` variables are public client configuration, and this repository documents this value as the actual Coinbase Developer Platform endpoint containing an API key. Once referenced by frontend code, the URL is embedded in the shipped JavaScript and can be extracted by any unauthenticated visitor. An attacker can then call the upstream CDP paymaster/bundler directly, bypassing the same-origin `/api/paymaster` proxy's session checks, allowlist validation, method filtering, sender quotas, and audit logging. Depending on CDP policy configuration, this can drain sponsorship quota/funds or sponsor unauthorized UserOperations.

title: EOA owner lane trusts tamperable add-owner previews
description: This commit wires `connectedOnchainEoaOwner` into `useAddOwnerFlow` and adds a fast path that submits `activePreview.txRequest` through the direct prepared-calls EOA-owner lane. However, `activePreview` may be restored from `sessionStorage`, and the client-side sanitizer only validates Relay user calls, not `txRequest`. The EOA lane does not re-fetch a fresh server preview, check the add-owner selector, check the owner being added, check value, or compare the transaction data against `preflight.ownerToAdd`. The downstream controller only verifies that `txRequest.to` equals the canonical CSW, then sends the arbitrary `data` using the public `VITE_CDP_SENDCALLS_PAYMASTER_URL` as a paymaster. A malicious authenticated user who controls an existing on-chain EOA owner of their CSW can tamper the persisted preview and cause the app/paymaster flow to sponsor arbitrary calls from their own CSW instead of only the intended owner-install transaction. This creates a sponsorship-drain / paymaster-policy bypass risk, especially if the direct CDP paymaster configuration is broader than the intended add-owner policy.

title: Custom owner token bypasses paymaster sender ownership checks
description: The new custom-owner policy handling is intended for the Relay Part 1 depository deposit path, but the implementation makes the token a broader bypass. In `validateSponsoredSmartWalletCalls`, once any valid custom-owner token is present, `assertSessionOwnsSender` is skipped for all call shapes, not only for the Relay Part 1 early-return path. For non-relay custom-owner calls, validation later accepts a self-call `addOwnerAddress(ownerToAdd)` based only on the token payload and does not re-check Coinbase Smart Wallet provenance or that the authenticated session owns `sender`. Separately, `_preview-add-owner` issues the token with `smartWalletAddress: relayFundingCswHint ?? cswAddress`; `relayFundingCswHint` is parsed but may be an arbitrary address and is not the same validated `relayQuoteUser` used to build the relay quote. An authenticated attacker can therefore request a preview with an arbitrary `relayFundingCswAddress`, receive a server-signed token for that address, and submit paymaster requests where `sender` is an attacker-controlled ERC-4337 account. Because the paymaster decodes only the outer ABI shape and no longer proves the sender is a Coinbase Smart Wallet/owned by the session in the custom-token path, a malicious account can implement compatible `execute`/`addOwnerAddress` selectors to run arbitrary expensive logic while receiving paymaster sponsorship.

title: Keeper control-plane endpoint bypasses queued policy checks
description: This commit adds /api/keeper/control-plane/operator-action as a routed API endpoint. The handler accepts any bearer with KPR_API_KEY, parses attacker-controlled action JSON, and immediately calls executeOperatorAction. Unlike the admin/control-plane queue path, this direct executor path does not require a valid operationId/stageId, does not verify that the job runner claimed the operation, and does not re-apply the keepr registry/degradation policy gate. For example, a caller with KPR_API_KEY can submit a vault.sweep action and choose an arbitrary ccaStrategyAddress; executeVaultSweep then signs and sends sweepCurrency() with KPR_PRIVATE_KEY to that supplied address. This expands compromise of the API key into direct use of the keeper signing key for out-of-band operator actions, bypassing the intended control-plane approval/queue policy.

title: Telegram webhook accepts lower-privileged shared secrets
description: The Telegram webhook endpoint authenticates incoming Telegram updates solely by comparing the x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token header to webhookConfig.webhookSecret. This commit changes webhookSecret from requiring TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET to falling back to TELEGRAM_BOT_CONFIG_SECRET and TELEGRAM_LINK_API_SECRET. Those fallback secrets are also used for other server-to-server Telegram endpoints via x-telegram-link-secret and are not necessarily scoped to authenticating Telegram-originated webhook traffic. If TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is omitted during a cutover, anyone with one of these lower-scoped shared secrets can POST arbitrary Telegram update JSON directly to /api/telegram/webhook. After the header check, the handler trusts the request body fields such as chat.id and from.id to determine whether the sender is an admin or whether the chat is allowed, then executes Telegram commands using that spoofed identity. This can enable forged admin/operator bot actions, account/trading flows, social actions, or other command execution paths that rely on Telegram webhook authenticity.

title: CI changes weaken secret protection
description: The new Cloudflare deployment workflow runs on pushes to main and on manual dispatch, then invokes `cloudflare/wrangler-action@v3` while passing `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` as action inputs. Because `@v3` is a mutable tag rather than a pinned commit SHA, a compromised or retagged upstream action can execute arbitrary code in the job with access to those Cloudflare credentials and deploy or modify the AlfaClub proxy worker. The same commit also adds top-level gitleaks allowlist entries for env/deploy-related historical paths and an entire historical directory; top-level allowlists skip all detectors, creating a credential-smuggling blind spot if real secrets appear in those paths.

title: Unpinned deploy actions can expose Cloudflare secrets
description: The added deploy workflow uses floating action references such as actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-node@v4, and pnpm/action-setup@v4 instead of pinning them to immutable commit SHAs. This repository's other workflows pin actions, which suggests this was an intended CI hardening practice. In this new job, any compromised or retagged action can persist malicious files or wrappers in the workspace before the deploy step. The later deploy step then exposes CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID and executes npx wrangler deploy from that workspace, allowing the compromised action to exfiltrate the Cloudflare token or alter the Worker deployment. Because the Worker proxies authenticated AlfaClub API traffic, a malicious deployment could also log forwarded Authorization headers and proxy secrets.

title: Unpinned Wrangler action can exfiltrate deploy secrets
description: The commit adds a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically deploys the AlfaClub Cloudflare Worker. Although `actions/checkout` is pinned to a full commit SHA, the deploy step uses `cloudflare/wrangler-action@v3`. GitHub action tags are mutable, so if the action repository, maintainer account, or tag is compromised or intentionally moved, the workflow will execute attacker-controlled code while providing it `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`. That code could exfiltrate the API token or deploy a malicious Worker. Because this Worker proxies authenticated AlfaClub traffic, a malicious deployment could also capture forwarded authorization headers and the proxy shared secret from live requests.

title: AMOE retries relay entries without charging credits
description: Before this commit, the retry handlers did not have a production relay wired and short-circuited when no test relay was injected. The commit now creates a production relay in both the cron and user retry endpoints and passes it into `retrySubmissionById*`. The shared retry executor relays the stored proof directly, but unlike the original submit path it does not transition the row to `broadcast` before relaying and it never consumes AMOE credits after a successful relay. In the original submit path, `ManagerDeclinedEntry` returns before the trailing credit debit, so a manager-declined submission in legacy single-call mode has not paid credits yet. When retried after conditions become favorable, the on-chain lottery entry can be accepted, but the retry code only calls `markSettled` and explicitly skips any debit. Because `markSettled` only accepts rows in `broadcast` or `proven` state, a retried `manager_declined` row also throws after the transaction has already been sent, leaving accounting inconsistent and potentially retryable. An authenticated user could create many manager-declined submissions while holding enough credits for the preflight check, then later obtain lottery entries without burning those credits.

title: Keepers can directly move Ajna vault assets without caps
description: AjnaERC4626Vault.moveFromBuffer, moveToBuffer, and move were previously restricted to the configured swapper/adapter. This commit changes them to onlySwapperOrKeeper, giving every AjnaVaultAuth keeper direct on-chain authority over position movement. The new automation stack stores maxAssetsPerMove and maxBucketStep in the database and the API uses maxAssetsPerMove when it calls moveFromBuffer, but those limits are not enforced by the contract and move/moveToBuffer are callable directly by the keeper address. A malicious or compromised keeper can therefore bypass /api/keeper/ajna/rebalance and move excess buffer assets or entire bucket LP balances to arbitrary allowed Ajna buckets, constrained only by minBucketIndex, available LP, and buffer-ratio checks for moveFromBuffer. This can degrade withdrawal liquidity, force exposure into unsafe buckets, and potentially cause loss of vault depositor funds depending on Ajna pool state.

title: Public Vite paymaster URL bypasses sponsorship proxy
description: Prepared-call sponsorship now reads `VITE_CDP_SENDCALLS_PAYMASTER_URL` from the frontend bundle and passes it directly as `capabilities.paymasterService.url`. Vite `VITE_*` environment variables are intentionally exposed to every browser client, so if this is configured with a CDP paymaster/bundler endpoint, any unauthenticated attacker can recover it from the built JavaScript and use it outside the app. This bypasses the same-origin `/api/paymaster` proxy, which exists to allowlist JSON-RPC methods, validate UserOperations, selectors, entrypoints, and rate-limit sponsorship. The helper also prioritizes this public env var even when callers pass `paymasterUrl: null`, so call sites that intended to disable paymaster sponsorship can unexpectedly include the direct sponsored endpoint whenever the env var is present. The result is a likely sponsorship-drain path unless equivalent restrictions are enforced upstream in CDP. The direct endpoint should remain server-side only, prepared-call sponsorship should go through a backend/proxy or short-lived scoped token, and `null` caller input should not be overridden by a public env var.

title: Launch script exposes production secrets to build tooling
description: scripts/launch.sh asks operators to export sensitive production variables such as AUTH_SESSION_SECRET, DATABASE_URL, DEPLOY_SESSION_TOKEN_HMAC_SECRET, PRIVY_APP_SECRET, PRIVY_WALLET_AUTHORIZATION_KEY, and DEPLOY_SOLANA_REGISTRATION_SECRET. It then runs pnpm install, lint, typecheck, generation, build, and forge commands in the same inherited environment. Any compromised dependency lifecycle/build step, malicious Vite/plugin code, or code pulled into the release branch can read process.env and exfiltrate those secrets. The script does use env -i for one Vitest invocation, but the higher-risk install/build/script commands before and after it are not sanitized. The safer pattern is to run dependency installation, linting, typechecking, tests, and builds in a secret-free environment, use --ignore-scripts or approved build scripts where possible, and only load production secrets for the narrow smoke-test commands that actually require them.

title: Keeper cron can leak KEEPR_API_KEY via derived base URL
description: The newly added /api/keeper/jobs/run endpoint is cron-authenticated and executes queued internal_api jobs. If KEEPER_COORDINATION_BASE_URL is not configured, getBaseUrl() builds the origin from req.headers.host and x-forwarded-proto without validating either value. runKeeperJobTick() then uses that baseUrl to fetch the queued path and attaches Authorization: Bearer <KEEPR_API_KEY>. A caller able to invoke the cron endpoint with CRON_SECRET, or a proxy/header confusion scenario where forwarded headers are attacker-controlled, can cause pending keeper jobs to be sent to an attacker-controlled origin and capture KEEPR_API_KEY plus job payloads. That key authenticates keeper coordination and keeper/CRE machine endpoints, so leakage can enable unauthorized operational job control or keeper action invocation. The safer behavior is to require a configured, allowlisted base URL for the server-side cron runner and reject untrusted forwarded host/proto values.

title: EOA owner signs unverified prepared UserOp hash
description: The commit changes self-auth owner installation to call submitOwnerInstallViaOnchainEoa. That lane sends the intended txRequest to a Coinbase-like cswRequest provider, but then blindly trusts the provider's returned signatureRequest.hash and userOp. The connected on-chain EOA owner is asked to personal_sign that opaque hash, and the unverified returned userOp is submitted via wallet_sendPreparedCalls. If the cswRequest provider or upstream wallet_prepareCalls response is compromised or malicious, it can ignore the requested addOwnerAddress(privyEoa) call, return a hash for an arbitrary UserOperation from the CSW, obtain a valid EOA-owner signature over that hash, and submit the arbitrary operation. Because the prompt is just personal_sign over a hash, the EOA owner does not get a reliable transaction preview. The client should decode and validate prepareResult.userOp, verify sender/chainId/callData/to/value against the server-prepared txRequest, and preferably recompute the UserOperation hash before requesting the EOA signature.

title: Workflow dispatch can leak the cron secret via branch code
description: The workflow adds both a scheduled trigger and workflow_dispatch, then checks out the triggering ref and runs frontend/scripts/alfaclub-auth-health-monitor.mjs with the repository secret ALFACLUB_HEALTH_CRON_SECRET in the environment. For workflow_dispatch runs, GitHub allows selecting a branch/ref, and actions/checkout defaults to that run ref. Therefore a lower-trust collaborator with write/workflow-dispatch ability can push a branch that changes the script to exfiltrate process.env.ALFACLUB_HEALTH_CRON_SECRET, manually dispatch this workflow on that branch, and obtain the cron secret. That secret is the same machine credential used to access cron-secret-gated production endpoints, so the workflow design turns branch write access into access to an operational secret. The workflow should either remove workflow_dispatch, use an environment secret restricted to protected branches with required approval, or avoid executing branch-controlled code with repository secrets.

title: Paymaster accepts unvalidated swap-proxy commands
description: The paymaster is a security boundary: it decides which UserOperations may receive gas sponsorship. This commit adds `SELECTOR_SWAP_PROXY_EXECUTE` and the hard-coded `UNISWAP_SWAP_PROXY_DEPLOY_ADDRESS` as an allowed swap target. However, unlike direct Universal Router calls, swap-proxy calls are not ABI-decoded, are not checked for canonical encoding, and do not enforce the existing Universal Router opcode allowlist. For `swap-proxy` and v3 paths, the code falls back to `assertRawSwapPayloadReferencesToken`, which only checks whether the token address bytes appear anywhere in calldata. After this weak check, `mode === 'swap'` returns early and skips the normal pass-2 target/selector validation. An authenticated/allowlisted attacker can therefore craft a sponsored UserOperation calling the swap proxy with arbitrary `commands`/`inputs` as long as the approved or wrapped token address is embedded somewhere in the payload. If the proxy forwards Universal Router commands, this can sponsor non-swap or disallowed commands and can be used to drain paymaster gas budget or abuse approvals/side effects that the paymaster intended to exclude. The fix is to decode the swap-proxy ABI, validate canonical encoding, enforce the same command/input opcode policy as Universal Router, and verify token in/out/amount/recipient semantics rather than doing a raw substring search.

title: Untrusted Zora wallet can override canonical CSW
description: When Privy returns exactly one smart-wallet candidate, the new fallback now asks Zora for profile wallets and returns the first EVM address that is not already known as a non-smart wallet in the Privy payload. That returned address is not required to be in Privy's smart-wallet candidate set, is not checked for Base smart-wallet bytecode, is not checked for ownership/control by the authenticated user, and is not checked for assignment to another profile. syncUserWallets then wraps that value as canonicalSmartWallet and persists it into the profile's canonical smart-wallet columns. Under the stated threat model where external API responses/metadata are attacker-controlled, a malicious Zora profile/API response can permanently pin an arbitrary address as the user's canonical CSW, misdirecting downstream identity, routing, and authorization decisions that trust accountSignals.canonicalCswAddress/csw_address.

title: Strategy caps can underprice shares and dilute incumbents
description: The commit adds a per-strategy cap by clamping each strategy's contribution to totalAssets(). However, the cap is not enforced against existing strategyDebt, new strategy deposits, auto-allocation, or the cap setter. This creates a public share-pricing attack whenever a capped strategy legitimately holds or reports more assets than the cap. During that period, ERC-4626 deposit/mint previews price new shares using the artificially low capped totalAssets(), so a depositor receives too many shares relative to the vault's true assets. If governance later raises or removes the cap, which the runbook explicitly anticipates during re-review, totalAssets() jumps and the attacker's discounted shares become claims on the previously unrecognized assets. The profit is paid by dilution of pre-existing shareholders. A safe design should prevent cap < strategyDebt/recognized principal, prevent allocation above a nonzero cap, or pause/block deposits while any active strategy is over cap before governance changes the cap.

title: Stale CSWs can be rebound to unauthorized profiles
description: The wallet sync path previously required a persisted canonical smart wallet to still be present in the live Privy-linked wallet classification before reusing it. This commit removes that live-link check and always normalizes/reinjects the persisted canonical CSW. In resolveCanonicalCsw, the commit also resolves a profile from raw Privy email/address hints before running syncUserWallets, then prefers the pre-sync persisted canonical over the freshly synced canonical and writes it to the post-sync profileId. If the hint-selected profile and the synced profile differ, or if a CSW was intentionally unlinked/rotated, a stale canonical CSW can be attached to the wrong/current account. Downstream authorization code treats profile_wallets/profiles canonical CSW rows as authority for deploy, paymaster, automation, and account operations, so resurrecting or misbinding a canonical CSW can grant unauthorized offchain privileges for another user's or a revoked wallet's account.

title: Same-origin IPFS rewrite enables XSS on 4626.fun
description: A new Vercel route rewrites `https://4626.fun/ipfs/<...>` to `https://pinata.4626.fun/ipfs/<...>` without a redirect status. In Vercel, this is a proxy rewrite, so the browser keeps origin `4626.fun` while rendering attacker-controlled IPFS bytes. This enables same-origin script execution if the CID resolves to HTML/JS content (or script-capable content), effectively creating an origin-confusion/XSS primitive on the primary domain. Impact is amplified because authentication uses shared-domain cookies (`.4626.fun`) and API auth falls back to cookie sessions, allowing malicious IPFS-hosted pages to perform authenticated same-origin API reads/actions as the victim.

title: Unrestricted randomness requests can drain Chainlink VRF funds
description:
The new `ChainlinkVRFAdapter.request()` function is externally callable and has no access control. The new `RandomnessRouter.acquireRequest()` is also externally callable and resolves a source for any arbitrary `creatorCoin` (falling back to default), then low-level-calls `request()` on that source.

In intended deployment, the adapter must be authorized in `CreatorVRFConsumerV2_5` as a local caller so it can request VRF. Once authorized, any attacker can repeatedly call either `ChainlinkVRFAdapter.request()` directly or `RandomnessRouter.acquireRequest(...)` to force paid VRF requests against the project subscription. This can drain LINK/subscription budget and prevent legitimate lottery draws (availability/economic DoS).

title: Arch B /coin sell trusts Zora quote for CSW calls
description: The Arch B /coin sell handler now fetches trade quotes from the Zora API and immediately uses the returned call target/data to build a Coinbase Smart Wallet UserOp. It also signs any Permit2 payloads supplied by the quote and re-quotes with those signatures. The code explicitly notes that a router allowlist is not wired. Since external API responses are attacker-controlled per the threat model, a malicious or tampered Zora response could supply an arbitrary call target and Permit2 details, leading the backend to sign approvals and submit a CSW call that drains assets. This is a new risk for the CSW path introduced by the commit.

title: Paymaster omits Zora min-output check server-side
description: The commit adds assertZoraFundingExecute(), which can reject funding calldata whose creator-coin amountOutMinimum is below the Sudoswap buy limit, and the frontend builder passes minOutputAmount: params.buyLimit. However, the server-side paymaster policy is the security boundary for sponsored UserOperations, and splitCanonicalEthFundingCalls() invokes assertZoraFundingExecute() without passing the Sudoswap input limit. The Sudoswap limit is decoded later, so no comparison is made between the Zora guaranteed output and the amount the sponsored Sudoswap buy is allowed to spend. The added paymaster test demonstrates this by accepting a batch whose Zora amountOutMinimum is 1n while the default buy limit is 1050n. An authenticated attacker can bypass the frontend and submit a crafted paymaster JSON-RPC request with under-guaranteed Zora funding. If the Zora swap produces less than the Sudoswap buy limit, the subsequent buy can revert while the paymaster still sponsors gas, enabling sponsorship-budget drain and unreliable sponsored execution.

title: Bribe claims can drain later epoch token balances
description: BribeDepot4626 accounts bribes per epoch in totalBribes[epoch][token], but it holds a single ERC20 balance per token for all epochs. The new claim logic computes the caller's entitlement from the old epoch accounting, then if that entitlement exceeds the depot's live token balance it sets amount = available and transfers that entire live balance. Because available is not scoped to the claimed epoch, an undercollateralized older epoch, for example due to a rebasing/deflationary bribe token or other balance shrinkage, can be used to drain tokens that were deposited for the current or later epochs. The claim is then marked claimed and claimedAmount is incremented only by the capped amount; rolloverExpiredEpoch can subsequently roll the unpaid accounting remainder forward without verifying that matching live tokens still exist, propagating insolvency. Prior to this commit, a claim whose calculated amount exceeded the live balance would normally revert instead of transferring all tokens currently held by the depot.

title: Reverting challenger can block impairment root recovery
description: This commit makes `challengeImpairmentRoot` payable and records `msg.sender` as the bond refund recipient. When management accepts a challenge via `clearImpairmentRootAfterChallenge`, or when the stale liveness valve resets the impairment trip, `_settleImpairmentChallengeBond(..., true)` attempts to refund the bond with a raw ETH call and reverts if that call fails. Because challenges are permissionless, an attacker can challenge from a contract whose `receive`/fallback always reverts. That makes the honest refund paths revert. If the challenge is submitted near the challenge-window close, management cannot clear the bad root and re-propose; the only immediate escape is `rejectImpairmentChallenge`, which slashes the bond but leaves the proposed root in place. During an active impairment the vault is in `VaultMode.Suspect`, and redeem/withdraw revert while the vault is not normal, so this can prolong an impairment freeze until timeout or force unsafe operational choices.

title: Recent Chip speaker fallback lets non-stakers suppress fades
description: This commit adds a fallback that, when a Chip/trade-completed card has no payload userAddress and no in-batch speaker, queries alfaclub.chat_ingest for the newest hex sender in the prior 2 hours. That lookup is not filtered by stake eligibility or by whether the sender is a plausible Chip trader. collectInverseAkitaChatTradeIntents then treats the first returned wallet as the sole attributed author and only falls back to the room creator if no wallet was returned. Later, executeInverseAkitaChatReaction checks that single selected sender's stake and rejects the intent if the sender is not eligible; it does not retry the next recent speaker or the room creator. Because the batch executor claims/dedupes the intent before execution, the legitimate Chip card can be recorded as rejected and not reprocessed. An attacker who can post in a configured AlfaClub reaction room can send any message from an unstaked wallet shortly before a narrow Chip card arrives, causing the new DB fallback to attribute the card to the attacker and skip the intended fade for up to the 2-hour lookback window. The fix should avoid allowing an ineligible DB speaker to block fallback, e.g. evaluate eligible candidates in order, fall through to the room creator on insufficient stake, or constrain durable speakers to stronger evidence of the actual Chip trader.

title: Remote lottery forwarder drops existing OFT entries
description: Remote ShareOFT users submit pending lottery entries by paying native LayerZero fees. The ShareOFT builds a payload containing six ABI fields, which is 192 bytes, sends it to the hub ShareOFT peer, and the hub ShareOFT forwards it to LotteryManager4626.receiveRemoteLotteryEntry. This commit changed receiveRemoteLotteryEntry to accept only exactly 224-byte V3 payloads and return early for any other length. Because the ShareOFT contracts were not updated to append a nonzero sourceEventId, all currently generated forwarded EVM remote lottery entries fail the new length check, emit InvalidPayloadReceived, and never reach _handleLotteryEntry. The remote pending entry has already been deleted before _lzSend, so the user loses the paid messaging fee and receives no VRF request or lottery chance.

title: Solana lottery amount scaling is missing
description: The commit enables live Solana lottery submissions, but `resolveAmountScaled` currently returns `amountRaw` unchanged and the worker submits `BigInt(row.amountScaled)` into the LayerZero payload. The Base lottery pricing code treats the payload amount as an 18-decimal ShareOFT/native token amount by computing `amount * price / 1e18`. Solana share-mesh mints are defaulted to 9 decimals in the provisioning script and can be configured with other decimals, so a default 9-decimal Solana buy is undercounted by 1e9 and may be skipped by `minSwapAmount`; conversely, a mint configured with more than 18 decimals would overstate lottery value and win probability. The submit path should persist/verify the Solana mint decimals and scale to the Base ShareOFT local decimals, failing closed on missing or unsafe scalar configuration.

title: payoutRecipient invariant can be bypassed by reverting reads
description: The new logic converts every failure while reading `creatorToken.payoutRecipient()` into `null` and then treats that as evidence that the asset is not a CreatorCoin. Because the mismatch/unresolved checks only run when the raw value is non-null, a contract whose `payoutRecipient()` reverts, a decoding error, or another read failure causes the deployment gate to silently skip this lane check. The deploy session handlers then allow post-phase2 progression whenever `violations.length === 0`. This weakens a security/economic invariant meant to ensure CreatorCoin external earnings are routed to the expected gauge or payout router. A safer implementation should only skip for a narrowly identified non-CreatorCoin/missing-selector case, or should record a blocking invariant violation when payout-recipient support cannot be verified for production deployments.

title: Spoofable rate limit protects new RPC fan-out
description: The wallet Zora holdings endpoint is public and now accepts extraTokens/extraTokenAddresses from the query string. Those addresses are normalized and, if recognized as Zora coins and absent from portfolio rows, cause the server to call balanceOf and decimals through configured Base RPC endpoints. This fan-out is bounded to 8 extra addresses, but each request can still consume Zora API quota, Base RPC quota, and serverless execution time. The only guard is a per-instance in-memory rate limit whose key is taken directly from x-forwarded-for before x-real-ip, so clients that can influence that header can rotate it to avoid the 40 requests/minute bucket. The spoofable rate-limit key existed before this commit, but the commit introduces the new attacker-controlled RPC fan-out protected by that weak limiter.

title: Chip username spoofing suppresses chat bridge fan-out
description: The new Chip detection helper returns true if either the sender is a known Chip system sender or the displayed username is `Chip`/`ChipBot`. That helper is then used by `fanOutInsertedRoomMessages` to remove messages from the relay set, and this commit also starts carrying live-message usernames into the inserted rows. As a result, a regular AlfaClub user whose profile/display username is `Chip` or `ChipBot` can have arbitrary messages persisted locally but not bridged to Telegram/XMTP. In cron command-only mode, the same username-only test also makes non-command messages eligible for ingestion as Chip cards. The code does not require the sender to be the non-wallet `trade-completed` system sender, does not require `isBot`, and does not validate that the text is a parseable Chip trade payload before suppressing fan-out. This creates a cross-channel visibility/audit bypass for user-controlled chat content.

title: Public cache stores session-specific chat access state
description: The commit changes /api/v1/alfaclub/room-timeline to derive chatAccess from the authenticated wallet and to include that object in the response. However, Cache-Control is selected only from includeChat. For an authenticated caller who lacks a room key or coin-equivalent access, includeChat is false, so the response is marked public with s-maxage=45 even though it contains session-specific chatAccess, including walletAddress and reason. A shared CDN/proxy can therefore cache a no-chat response for a signed-in no-access wallet and serve it to other users requesting the same URL. This can leak a requester's wallet/access status and can temporarily deny legitimate keyholders access to chatEvents by cache poisoning them with a cached no-access response. The endpoint should use private/no-store whenever a session/auth context influenced chatAccess, omit personalized chatAccess from publicly cached responses, or vary on Cookie/Authorization.

title: Legacy salt selectors bypass vanity entitlement check
description: This commit replaced the deploy-session Phase-1 selector constants with CURRENT_DEPLOYMENT_BATCHER_SELECTORS, which contains only the new v1.19.1 selectors. The entitlement gate calls hasPhase1SaltOverrideCalls() and only treats calls as salt overrides if their selector is in PHASE1_WITH_SALT_SELECTORS. Legacy salted selectors such as 0x297cb1e6, 0x4154f24e, and 0x3bc09a8b are no longer in that set, so legacy salted calldata is ignored and phase1UsesSaltOverride becomes false. If the request does not declare a paid custom shareSuffix, the share vanity entitlement is not required. However, the paymaster still explicitly allowlists and decodes the legacy salted batcher selectors, so these calls remain executable/sponsorable. This creates an authorization/paywall bypass for custom ShareOFT salt overrides on legacy-compatible batchers.

title: Raw market symbols added to LLM prompt allow prompt injection
description: The new prompt-building behavior maps `availableMarkets` to `market.symbol` and joins those values directly into the LLM user message. These symbols are derived from Hyperliquid metadata (`allPerpMetas`) where `nameRaw` is only trimmed/case-normalized, with no character, newline, or length validation before being stored as `symbol`. If an attacker can poison or influence the external market metadata response, a symbol can contain prompt-control text such as newlines and instructions. When the LLM classifier is enabled, that injected text is placed before the chat message in the prompt and can steer the classifier to emit a valid trade JSON for a benign message. The resulting LLM classification is accepted as a parsed trade intent and later used by the trading path, subject to existing room, author, allowlist, and trading checks. Those downstream checks reduce impact, but they do not prevent the classifier from being manipulated into creating unintended trade intents for otherwise eligible chat activity.

title: Phase2 paymaster skips vault provenance checks
description: The changed paymaster validation now initializes vaultValidated to true whenever mode === 'deploy_phase2'. For finalizePhase2 calls, expectedCodeIds are normally absent, so the CREATE2 validation is not performed; because vaultValidated is already true, the Phase1Deployed log fallback is also skipped. The only remaining offchain checks for deploy_phase2 are that vault/wrapper/shareOFT bytecode exists and that view functions report matching vault/share/asset addresses. Those checks can be satisfied by attacker-deployed mock contracts, and owner() mismatches are only enforced if owner() returns successfully.
